Apartment D Films’ Cami Kwan discusses the intricate process behind the handcrafted film.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The fight for the Christmas advert crown is on, and brands have set standards high this year. From hand-drawn animation to immersive storytelling, there's been a wonderful display of hand-crafted creativity, and among the ranks, beauty brand e.l.f. did not disappoint.

As the brand's first-ever holiday campaign, the beautiful stop-motion animation is a sparkling debut that captures the joy of the festive season. A masterful display of tactile craftsmanship, the 'e.l.f. Made to Stand Out' campaign carries many of the traits of the best Christmas adverts, proving that analogue storytelling is the perfect tool for sparking festive joy.

Narrated by iconic actor Alan Cumming, the campaign follows friends Kit, Echo and Cleo as they reunite in their hometown for a holiday get-together. What could be an uncomfortable hangout turns into a celebration of the qualities that make them extraordinary, spreading festive cheer.

“For a campaign about the power of standing out, the medium needed to stand out too, and stop motion felt like such a natural fit for this story," explains Oshiya Savur, chief marketing officer at e.l.f. Beauty. "We're seeing a real appetite for nostalgia and a return to simpler times, with 72% of Americans saying nostalgic memories inspire them when life feels complicated.

There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand

There's something about stop motion that takes you right back to the holiday specials you grew up watching, but we saw an opportunity to give that familiar art form a uniquely e.l.f. twist. There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand, and when you combine that with our signature wit and wink, you create something that feels both familiar and completely unexpected.”

Created by Apartment D Films, each element of the ad reads as a love letter to analogue craft, from individually moulded characters to intricately constructed miniature sets. "We used a wide variety of different materials! It's truly a mixed media project," Cami Kwan, Creative Director of Apartment D, tells Creative Bloq. "The puppets have aluminium and steel wire armatures inside, which makes them posable. Their hands and heads are made of printed resin, which we then painted and finished with actual e.l.f. products! The cheeks and mouths of the puppets are colored using a combination of e.l.f. Powder Blush Palette, e.l.f Perfect 10 Eyeshadow Palette, and e.l.f. Halo Glow Silky Powder Highlighter.

All the characters' hair is made with different weights and textures of yarn, to call back to super nostalgic toys, but with a modern sensibility. The eyebrows and eyelids of the characters are made of a mix of wax and clay, so they're super mouldable to get big expressions in the performance, and also so you can literally see the animators' fingerprints on the characters as they emote.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

A lot of the world around the character is made of wood, but with hand-painted textures so the wood grain is more painterly and stylized. The mini products and bottles the characters use are all hand-sculpted out of clay, and then finished with a variety of nail art techniques, like cured acrylic, gels, and powder shimmers! The mini bottles are really so, so small; none of them is more than 1 inch tall."

It wasn't a project without some difficulties, as Cami explains. "One of our challenges was integrating real beauty products intended to live on human skin with stop-motion puppets. Unlike real humans, our puppets don't have pores and don't have a body temperature, both of which e.l.f. beauty products are chemically formulated to interact with.

On top of that, stop motion puppets are designed to be handled and touched constantly during the animation process, so the treatments and colors on them need to be incredibly resilient to constant wear and tear. We spent a good deal of time on the material testing of the e.l.f. beauty products to see which ones would integrate best with our fabrication techniques.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analog, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world

It was actually really interesting to let our puppet team dip into their extensive knowledge of material science! We've found that generally anything based in a powder pigment merged really well with our typical techniques, and those combinations were really successful in getting puppets with a lot of character and a lot of dynamic color and shimmer on screen!"

Honouring such a tactile animation style is a time intensive practice, but are audiences hungry for analogue creativity? “Absolutely," says Oshiya. "The more purely AI-generated content we see, the greater the opposite and equal reaction from people craving something real: human connection and creativity they can actually feel.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analogue, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world. At e.l.f., we're human first, human last. AI can be an incredible tool, but taste, discernment and original ideas come from human ingenuity. At the end of the day, we want to make people feel something, and that human element is what makes it possible.”

"The thing I'm most proud of is how kind and collaborative our crew on this project was. It's not something you can point to on screen, but it's something you can feel in how much care was taken with every frame, and how lively the animation is. There was so much joy in the creation and filming of this project, and I do think you can feel that in how kinetic and inventive everything is. It's a little zany, a little imperfect, and really so captivating when all seen together!" says Cami.

Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection.

"For a more specific on-screen detail, though, I love the smear frames we used when Echo is zooming between the tables and getting everyone amped up! Smear frames are an animation technique that's most typical in 2D animation – they're moments when, for just a few frames, you distort the character and literally smear them to give a sense of speed, mimicking the way something moving too fast on a live-action camera will appear blurry.

You hardly ever see smear frames in stop motion, but one of the things that we really focus on at Apartment D is pushing the stylistic boundaries of stop motion and finding ways to bring 2D animation techniques into our three-dimensional medium. So, in that Echo zooming scene, we actually used pieces of cut paper to create practical, dimensional smear frames! Jen Prokopowicz, the animator of that shot, curved the paper smears to get an extra sense of dimension, and created smears of different sizes to get a sense of speeding up and slowing down. It's just so cool, and something that generally only real animation nerds will notice," Kami adds.

“At e.l.f., we've never been interested in being part of a sea of sameness. We're a brand that celebrates the unexpected, embraces individuality and believes that what makes us different is what makes us extraordinary. That's what I love about stop motion. Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection. Just as no two handcrafted creations are exactly alike, no two people are either. It's a playful way to bring our belief in celebrating every eye, lip and face to life, and a reminder that your difference is low-key your gift,” says Oshiya.

#9107. Jordan Poorman Cocker’s Vision of Global Indigeneity

The curator, who just organized a major rehang of Indigenous art at Crystal Bridges, reflects on the ways institutions can create space for Native artists to flourish.

BENTONVILLE, Ark. — On October 16 and 17, before a room full of Indigenous artists, curators, and scholars at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art’s symposium on contemporary Native art, Jordan Poorman Cocker opened with a land acknowledgment. Founded by Walmart heiress Alice Walton, the museum sits on the ancestral homelands of the Osage Nation, Quapaw Nation, and Caddo Nation, who were forcibly relocated in the 19th century. Poorman Cocker, a Kiowa and Tongan citizen, was hired as the museum’s Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) officer and first full-time curator of Indigenous art in 2023. She makes the hour-and-a-half drive in from Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the Cherokee Nation’s capital and home to several nations coerced there during the removal era.

The two-day gathering coincided with the reinstallation of contemporary Native art in the museum, which Poorman Cocker spearheaded alongside Art Bridges Curator Ashley Holland (Cherokee Nation) as a way to showcase the diversity of style, medium, and living Native artists across Indian Country, including works by citizens of the ancestral Tribes in Arkansas. Choctaw and Cherokee multi-disciplinary artist Jeffrey Gibson delivered a keynote address, and later spoke to an audience with Poorman Cocker while beading; Diné weaver Melissa Cody traced the lineage of her work in dialogue with her mother Lola Cody; and Lehuauakea delivered a workshop based in her traditional kapa practice.

Poorman Cocker’s own curatorial practice draws on her background in museum studies at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand and the global spirit of Indigeneity, which rejects the divisive borders of colonial nation-states. Like many Native curators, she cites the groundbreaking 2019 exhibition Hearts of Our People: Native Women Artists at the Minneapolis Institute of Art as a major source of inspiration. That sentiment was echoed by Kiowa beadwork artist Terri Greeves, who spoke at the symposium alongside other Kiowa Tribe members and matriarchs. Poorman Cocker is also a beadwork and textile artist herself, rooted in Kiowa and Tongan beadwork and textile conventions.

In an email correspondence with Hyperallergic, Poorman Cocker shared more about a recent landmark commission, telling a fuller history of Native art, and what it means to bring Kiowa voices into the museum. The interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

Hyperallergic: Tell me more about what the reinstallation at Crystal Bridges represents for Indigenous art in this moment. What is it trying to change? How did the 114,000-square-foot expansion inform the museum’s capacity to provide ongoing opportunities to collaborate with the featured artists?

JPC: The impetus is to recenter two primary areas: the Indigenous art collection and the craft collection. Native American and Indigenous art are foundational to every American art collection. Over the years, I have written acquisition proposals for artworks sourced from the gallery system and annual markets, with an emphasis on artist commissions.  Crystal Bridges is better positioned to nourish the art ecosystem, including many artists — particularly those whose work aligns with intergenerational art forms, who need financial support for artist apprenticeships, community classes, and other art education efforts that sustain artist communities and knowledge systems.

Indigenous and Native art makes up about 3% of Crystal Bridges’s permanent collection. The museum sector writ large has a long way to go to better present Indigenous artists and stories.

#9106. DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch

A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."

WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project.

Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction.

At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia, the Arlington County Board, as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch.

We've been covering Black Friday iPad deals for as long as I can remember (12 solid years to be exact!), and during all the time I've been involved, I've been a champion for the mid-tier iPad Air.

But annually increasing capabilities, and largely a price freeze, has meant that it's no longer my idea of the best iPad around anymore. That title now goes to the (not really that) humble iPad. The A16, 2025 version, to be precise.

Right now, you can buy the 11-inch, A16-chipped iPad for $399 over at Amazon, in what is the earliest Black Friday iPad deal that I've seen. I've got both this model and the most recent Air, and though I still enjoy the Air more, for the money, the entry-level iPad is the only one I would buy today.

This is my new go-to recommendation to 80% of Creative Bloq readers. For those of you who edit video, then you'll need the Air or more likely the Pro. For artists, the Air is still the best option overall. But for the vast majority of use, the 2025 iPad is the ideal tablet, especially at $399!

This is my all-time favourite iPad, and I like it more than the classic iPad mainly because I know that it's quicker, smoother and brighter... not that I particularly notice all of that in my everyday use. When it comes to professional use, digital artists should definitely choose between this and the Pro. Value for money makes this my pick.

The iPad Pro is my least favourite iPad, and that's because I'm not a video editor or professional digital artists, so I have no need for its immense power. But then, even when you consider its potential, I just feel that it's a heavy tablet that's way over-priced. The Air and the classic iPad will always appeal over the Pro for me.

#9104. Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial

Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company.

Meg Onli, an organizer behind some of the Whitney Museum of American Art's signature exhibitions, and Zack Winokur, a performing arts director and co-founder, are the co-curators for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, the museum announced today, November 6.

“Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art," Scott Rothkopf, director of the Whitney, said in a statement. "Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial."

The news comes just two months after the 2026 Biennial closed and a month after unionized staff at the museum dodged a full-blown strike ahead of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, a blockbuster retrospective co-curated by Onli. The Whitney union was one of four New York City museum unions under United Auto Workers 2110 — along with the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — that voted to strike amid drawn-out contract negotiations over low compensation, benefits, and workplace conditions. Hours before the planned strike, unionized staffers ratified their second contract and secured a new wage floor, increased parental and bereavement leave, and stronger safety provisions, among other amendments.

First joining the museum as curator-at-large in 2023, Onli co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Even Better Than the Real Thing, with Chrissie Iles. That same year, Onli was promoted to Nancy and Fred Poses Curator to lead the Whitney’s painting and sculpture acquisition committee, bringing her previous experience as director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles and associate curator at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania.

“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about," Onli said in a statement. "I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead."

Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company, an interdisciplinary collective comprised of 17 singers, musicians, dancers, and other performing artists. He also served as artistic director for Little Island on Pier 55 and NYPopsUp, a statewide initiative aimed at opening performing arts spaces after COVID-19.

“I’m honored to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur added in a statement. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring."

Dating back to 1932, the Whitney Biennial remains the longest-running survey of American art, with more than 3,600 artists participating in the exhibition to date. The 83rd edition is slated to open in March 2028.

#9103. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which was designed by Nike with a pattern of “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

Compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

Investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

The Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

At a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

The following table shows how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

Notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

The 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

Consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

The single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

The historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

When you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and new highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

More frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

#9101. London’s National Gallery publishes recommendations of its citizens’ assembly

The recommendations comes as the museum plans for a major new extension

The National Gallery in London says in a new report that a new public body founded to advise the UK national museum on its future policy and direction has given it “a mandate to be brave”.

The new initiative, titled NG Citizens, was announced in July last year. The museum aims to transform its governance model by launching a citizens’ assembly made up of members of public from across the UK.

The accompanying report outlines the recommendations and shared vision developed by 55 participants who took part in five sessions between November 2025 and March 2026.

The new assembly recommended that the museum should “embrace and grow commercial opportunities” and also use technology to support personalised itineraries, especially for “under-represented” groups, among other objectives.

Other key recommendations for the museum include being more informative about its wider history, representation and context behind the art. The collection also urgently needs to be a true reflection of the UK, said the assembly members.

The overarching question put to the assembly members was: “What do you want from the UK’s National Gallery? How can it bring people and paintings together in authentic and meaningful ways, now and in the future?” A series of eight principles, defined as the “core values that guide how the gallery can move towards the vision”, were discussed at the sessions.

Core challenges on the agenda included: “How can the National Gallery balance its role as a free public gallery whilst being commercially minded? What is the social value of art? How can art galleries explain and support this? Can art ever be open to everyone?” Other issues discussed include “how to bring in new, diverse and loyal audiences.”

Over the next four years, a series of smaller panels, made up of assembly members, will work directly with the gallery to oversee the implementation of these ideas. “NG Citizens will now continue into its second phase: the Citizens’ Panel. The panel will consist of three separate cohorts between 2026 and 2030,” says the report.

Some issues were not up for discussion at the sessions says the report, such as ideas that would result in significant changes to existing buildings; ideas that involve buying or selling paintings; and ideas that might compromise the gallery’s role as an arm’s length body of the UK government.

The report concludes: “The National Gallery was the first of its kind to do this on this scale, in the world. We can accept it was never going to be perfect; it would present challenges, but we hope observers can learn from our experience… To have a group of people that we can work with over future years, who will maintain a critical and supportive perspective, presents opportunities far beyond the usual focus group approach.”

Maurice Davies, a UK culture consultant at Cultural Associates Oxford, says the report is “quite remarkable” but questions whether the National Gallery will be “bold and brave enough” to take forward the assembly’s recommendations.

He tells The Art Newspaper: “The panel have concluded that the gallery needs to be far more than it currently is; a collection of European paintings based in the centre of London. They say the collection ‘urgently’ needs to be far more diverse and to represent the diversity of the UK so it needs to change its collecting policy significantly.

And they say the gallery should share ‘paintings and resources’ throughout the UK which suggests the gallery might want to reconsider its current hugely expensive project to extend its building in central London in favour of using resources to work with museums and galleries in a wide range of locations.”

Last September, the National Gallery received pledges of £150m each (from Michael Moritz’s Crankstart foundation and the Julia Rausing Trust) for its planned major new extension scheduled for completion in the early 2030s.

Discover whether you need a basic iPad, Air, Pro or mini.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Choosing an iPad used to be a piece of cake. Now there are four families, different processors, and prices that jumped up in June 2026. So it’s important to pick the right one, and not pay through the nose for power you don't actually need.

The good news is, for browsing, streaming, gaming and a bit of sketching, the classic 11-inch iPad (2025) does everything you probably need. If you have specific tasks beyond that, it might be worth shelling out for a more expensive iPad Air, iPad Pro and iPad mini. But for most people (including me) this is the best iPad to get.

Below, I’ve compared the latest versions of all four models – because they are the best versions of all the families – drawing on both my own experience and reviews by the Creative Bloq team, which has been using iPads since Gen 1 in 2010.

Our top pick for most people is what people often call the basic iPad. But don't let that put you off, because "basic" is purely a relative term here. So yes, this is the cheapest iPad Apple sells, but it’s still a lovely tablet to use every day. Web browsing, streaming, video calls, note-taking and email are all fast and easy, and the bright, colourful screen is big enough to be comfortable without weighing you down.

It’s a decent gaming tablet too, as long as you're not set on playing AAA titles at the highest frame rates. Call of Duty Mobile runs okay, for instance, until you go up to 120fps mode, while Infinity Nikki might need dropping to medium. The lack of an M-series chip also locks you out of some games entirely.

For drawing, though, it does the job nicely. Add an Apple Pencil and you can sketch happily in Procreate, although the first-generation Pencil is the one to get, as the cheaper USB-C model doesn’t have pressure sensitivity. As our reviewer Ian Evenden says: “You don’t get desktop-level processing power, but you do get one of the friendliest, most useful tablets around, especially if you combine it with a Pencil for sketching.”

A couple more things to point out: there’s no Apple Intelligence, the USB-C port is slow and the screen has an air gap beneath the glass, so it feels a little less refined under a stylus. In short, the compromises are there... but they won't be deal-breakers for most people. Finally, bear in mind that reports suggest a replacement could arrive in early 2027 – although Apple hasn’t confirmed anything so that's currently just speculation.

The Air costs $300 / £320 more than the basic iPad. In return you get a much faster chip, twice the memory, Apple Intelligence, Apple Pencil Pro support and the option of a 13-inch screen.

That extra power is overkill if all you want to do on your iPad is check emails and watch Netflix. But if you want to run demanding creative software or games, then it may be worth it. In our Geekbench 6 tests, the M4 Air’s multi-core score of 13,168 was more than double the 6,338 we got from the basic iPad. Its graphics score of 53,071 also matched the 53,252 of the previous M4 iPad Pro.

That will really make a difference, for example, if you want to run 3D software. Our reviever, Glen Southern, who has used iPad Pros for professional work since they launched, found that he could sculpt models of up to 16 million polygons in Nomad Sculpt. But he cautions that for some, all that power will be overkill. “For a lot of creative users, 12GB of memory and an M4 chip may be more iPad than they’ll ever actually need,” he says.

On the other side of the equation, the Air isn't quite as capable as the Pro. For instance, it has an LCD screen rather than OLED, and a 60Hz refresh rate rather than 120Hz. For many people, though, that line won’t be worth paying to cross.

The Pro is the absolute best tablet Apple makes, and so if price is no object then please, knock yourself out. It is very expensive, though, and for most people, it’ll be total overkill. However, if you have a specific work need for a Pro such as 3D modelling or video editing, then it may be worth the investment. And it truly is a lovely thing to have and use.

The tandem OLED screen is the best on any iPad, with deep blacks, high contrast and a 120Hz refresh rate. And it’s the most powerful iPad by a distance, scoring 16,443 for multi-core and 74,046 for graphics in our Geekbench 6 tests. “Whether it’s for building up a lot of layers in Procreate or Illustrator, video editing in Final Cut Pro or Davinci Resolve or crazy stuff in Zbrush or Nomad Sculpt, the M5 iPad Pro barely breaks a sweat,” says our reviewer Ian Evenden.

That price, though, is not to be sneezed at. And the cost climbs quickly once you add a Magic Keyboard, Apple Pencil Pro and extra storage. So unless you're certain exactly what the Pro would do for you, we'd say: get the Air.

The iPad mini is, just as the name suggests, small and light. That makes it a great choice if you want something you can carry easily in a small bag. It's also useful for using in tight spaces, like a crowded railway carriage.

If you’re a fan of small, and you want the best, the 2026 version is the one to choose. It's the first mini with an OLED screen, the first with IP67 water and dust resistance, and at 255g, it’s noticeably lighter than its predecessor.

We haven’t tested it ourselves yet, but our sister site TechRadar praised both its screen and fast performance. So if you want an iPad for reading, travel, note-taking and sketching on the go, it's a great choice; especially if you opt for the paper-like nano-texture screen, which costs an extra $100 / £100 on the 256GB and 512GB models.

The catch? It's a whopping $250 / £270 more than the basic iPad and only $50 / £50 less than the 11-inch Air, so you really are paying a premium for the smallness. The 8.5-inch screen is also stuck at 60Hz. However, if you want to save some cash and the upgrades aren't important to you, retailers still have the previous A17 Pro model, which has dropped to a record low.

The best iPad overall is the iPad Pro, which is number three on our list above. It's the fastest, most powerful and has the best screen. So if money's no object, this the one you should buy, unless you're mainly interested in something small and portable (in which case, go for the iPad mini, number four on our list.) However, if you don't have endless cash to spare, the iPad Pro may well be overkill, so it's worth deciding whether you really need all that power. The basic iPad is much cheaper and, as discussed below, is actually the best pick for most people.

The basic iPad (which is just called "iPad" on Apple's website and retailer listings) is the one most people should buy. It’s by far the cheapest way to get a new iPad, and handles browsing, streaming, email, video calls and casual gaming with ease. If you don't want to do anything more complicated with an iPad, there's no reason to pay more. It's number one on our list above.

The basic iPad, number one on our list above, is the best choice for most students, if you just want it for low-powered tasks like taking notes, reading, checking emails, listening to music and watching video. If you study a creative subject or use demanding apps, though, the iPad Air is worth the extra money if your budget allows.

The basic iPad with an Apple Pencil is the affordable way to start with drawing on the iPad. If you’d like a better drawing experience, the Air gives you a laminated screen, Apple Pencil Pro support and the option of a 13-inch canvas. For more detail, see our guide to the best iPads for drawing.

The iPad Pro, number 3 on our list, is the one to get if you need its OLED screen, 120Hz refresh rate or maximum power. But check that you really do. Many professionals will be just as happy with the 13-inch Air. Our guide to the best iPad for Procreate goes into more detail.

#9099. Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center

Upon his appointment, the artist reflected on the urgency he feels to “make sense of rapidly unfolding events, question prevailing narratives, and imagine alternative futures.”

Artist, educator, and writer Pablo Helguera has been appointed as the new director of the New School's Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC), succeeding Senior Director and Chief Curator Carin Kuoni, who steered the arts-driven research center for 22 years. Helguera was also tapped as the director of the university's art collection, which consists of over 2,000 postwar and contemporary works.

Having entered the new role this Monday, November 2, Helguera takes the reins after six years of serving as an assistant professor and director of the Arts Management and Entrepreneurship graduate program at the New School's College of Performing Arts. Helguera was previously the director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art for over a decade.

As an artist, Helguera centers social engagement through public performance and installation, archival findings, pedagogical practices, and traditional media. Among his most famous projects is “The School of Panamerican Unrest” (2006), a cross-continental road trip from Anchorage, Alaska, to Ushuaia, capital of Argentina's southernmost Tierra del Fuego province, that culminated in over 100 public engagement events across 25 cities in 20 countries. Helguera is also known for developing Librería Donceles, a traveling used bookstore with thousands of Spanish-language texts that visited 13 countries.

The social, ideological, and cultural frameworks of language are prominent themes that Helguera explores in his practice, which coalesces with his roles in education and public programming. He became a Guggenheim Fellow in 2008, and additional recognitions include support from the Franklin Furnace Archive, Art Matters, and Blade of Grass; a Creative Capital grant; and an honorary doctorate from the Kansas City Art Institute.

#9098. The Jewish Sisters in Renoir’s “Pink and Blue”

Author Catherine Ostler follows the lives of the two cherubic girls, whose rarefied lives in an elite, artistic French family would be toppled by the horrors of the Holocaust.

In 1881, at the dawn of the Belle Époque, Pierre-Auguste Renoir steps into the ritzy Parisian townhouse of the Cahen d’Anvers family to paint a double portrait of four-year-old Alice and six-year-old Elisabeth, daughters of the Antwerp-born Jewish banker Louis and salonnière Louise. In the finished canvas, “Pink and Blue, the Misses Cahen d’Anvers” (1881), the two cherubic girls with rosy cheeks and reddish-golden hair stand in a sumptuous salon, holding hands, enveloped in a cloud of lace and satin.

This “duet of sugared-almond-colored-sweetness,” as author Catherine Ostler puts it, and “La Petite Irène” (1880) — a portrait of their older sister, painted by the artist a year earlier — are the springboard for her book The Renoir Girls.

From the opening pages, Ostler’s exhaustively researched, deftly structured book conjures the gilded world of fin-de-siècle Paris, leading the reader through the brocade curtains of the Cahen d’Anvers family’s dazzling life as members of the Jewish elite to their tragic end in the Holocaust. At center stage is the art patron Louise; Marcel Proust was a close friend, and her famed salon drew artists, writers, and members of the conservative Catholic aristocracy alike. And there was her lover, the collector and art critic Charles Ephrussi, who had arranged for Renoir to paint the girls and was suspected of being Alice's biological father. But alongside this world of opulence and privilege, in which every ball and horse race the Cahen d’Anvers women attended made it into the newspaper columns, ran another Paris, one divided by inequality and political instability, which fueled antisemitism and punctured the sisters’ rarefied lives.

Ostler captures the collision of these two worlds with the dreadful inevitability of a train derailing in slow motion. Despite the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Code having ensured equal rights for France’s Jewish population, antisemitism was insidious across the country. It took the form of resentful grumbles “aligned with the times”: “I really give up with the Jews,” wrote Renoir to a friend complaining about Louis’s “stingy” payment. It took the form of the anti-Jewish venom of diarist and, perversely, frequent visitor to Louise’s salon, Edmond de Goncourt. And it reached its peak with the Dreyfus Affair of 1894 to 1906, in which a Jewish French army officer was framed for treason. While the Cahen d’Anvers and their close circle belonged to the Dreyfusard camp, some members of the Jewish elite — the haute Juiverie — seemed to waltz through this moral and political crisis, which polarized the nation. Amid political assassinations and anarchist bombs, Louise and Louis went on worshiping the 18th century and restoring Château Champs-sur-Marne to its ancient regime glory. Meanwhile, the girls continued on their path to assimilation, not without puzzling twists and heartbreaks.

In 1895, at the height of the Dreyfus Affair, a 21-year-old Elisabeth converts to Catholicism and marries a penniless aristocrat, whom she later divorces. In 1897, the adventurous, anglophile Alice meets the ambitious British Colonel Charles Townshend in Egypt and, a year later, ties the knot in an Anglican ceremony at her parents' chateau. And Irène, the only one to enter into an arranged marriage, leaves her husband, Moïse de Camondo, for the head of his stable. But in the 1930s, the glittering carousel comes to a screeching halt, and Ostler’s account of the Nazis’ occupation descends into a harrowing tale of persecution.

The Cahen d'Anvers’s love for France and desire to belong run deep throughout the book. Their forebears adapted their surname to sound more aristocratic; Irène’s son, Nissim de Camondo, fought for France and died in World War I. They gave generously to philanthropic causes, restored dilapidated historical properties, and later donated them to the French state. But neither their wealth nor their belief in the values of the Enlightenment could shield them from the catastrophe to come, and four members of the family perished in concentration camps, including Elisabeth, who, in 1944, old and infirm, was betrayed by the mayor of the village where she was hiding and died in or on the way to Auschwitz.

As for the paintings, “Pink and Blue” now hangs at the Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, where it is one of the institution’s most popular works. “La Petite Irène,” on the other hand, was looted by the Nazis, restituted to Irène, and then was subsequently bought by the Swiss arms dealer and war profiteer Emil Georg Bührle. It is now on view at the Kunsthaus Zürich, its sweetness belying a story of devastation and betrayal amid one of the darkest chapters of European history — a story Ostler’s engrossing, kaleidoscopic chronicle vividly brings to life.

#9097. Please Don’t Sit on the Flowers

Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape goes to auction, Brancusi gets lost at MoMA, interview with Doris Salcedo, and is showing at documenta worth it?

Sitting at September Cafe, I watch the autumn leaves separate from the trees and get carried away gently by the wind. They swirl and twirl, performing a merry little dance in the air before falling to their final resting place.

News has just come in about a sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections, as fierce and awesome as a Gustave Courbet wave. But I see nobody popping champagne bottles in the streets. A pregnant black cat with a hanging belly saunters by.

Lying back in the dentist’s chair, a TV screen in front of me shuffles picturesque views from exotic places. They're idyllic to the point of not looking real. My doctor, a Lebanese, shows me an X-ray of my mouth, which looks like Beirut at the height of the Civil War.

The sky over the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge is gray, and the Harlem River is brooding as I make my way to Taryn Simon’s exhibition Father Country I Do Love You at the Guggenheim Museum. The show tells the heroic tales of an FBI agent whose alleged career intersects with major events in American history. Cold, antiseptic photographs encased neatly in plexiglass make up a detective story linking the protagonist to the explosion of TWA Flight 800, the 9/11 attacks, the bombing of the United States embassy in Nairobi, Bill Clinton’s impeachment, and more. Trudging up the Guggenheim’s spiraling galleries, I wonder whether this patriotic show is organized and sponsored by the US State Department. Simon makes you read a lot, but all that reading is just meant to distract you from thinking.

Jodie Foster narrates the audio guide for those who don’t have the patience to read long-winded wall texts. At the cafeteria, while eating a bikini sandwich, I see a woman who looks exactly like Judi Dench, another actress. “I love storytelling,” she tells a friend before plunging her teeth into a chocolate croissant.

On my way out, I once again resent how this museum forces everyone to exit through the gift shop to encourage commerce, but I buy myself a $5 Guggenheim bag anyway. Outside, in one of the manicured gardens of the Upper East Side, a small sign pleads, “Please don’t sit on the flowers.”

I cross the street into Central Park through Engineers’ Gate, climb the steps past a gilded bust of John Purroy Mitchel, NYC mayor between 1914-1918, and look out over the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir. I think of the Kennedys, of Trump, and of Simon. A worker collects brown leaves in plastic bags and tosses them into a truck wrapped in a photo of green leaves. A mother tries to snap a photo of her child, but the unruly kid refuses to pose for the camera. He throws a fit, falls, and, to her shock, ends up sitting on the flowers.

#9096. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.

Elon Musk is winding down production, and I won’t be shedding a tear.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tesla is winding down Cybertruck production. Elon Musk has confirmed that manufacturing at the Texas Gigafactory will scale back around mid-2027 to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis. And so ends one of the strangest design experiments in automotive history, one riddled with ugly mistakes and design fails.

Okay, ‘ends’ might be jumping the gun a little. Elon Musk hasn’t said outright that the Cybertruck is being discontinued, and it’s not clear whether production could move elsewhere. But as posted on X, Texas is the only known facility equipped to build its rather specialised parts, so the writing is pretty clearly on the wall.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab productionNovember 6, 2026

It was always going to be a tough sell. When Musk unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019, he promised a revolution in pickup design. What we got looked like it had rolled straight out of a dystopian sci-fi movie: angular stainless steel, sharp edges and a comically oversized windscreen with one comically oversized, slow wiper. Different? Absolutely. I’ll give it that.

The reaction was instant, with designers and the internet having a field day. We covered the fallout in our 2019 look at the designers taking aim at Tesla’s Cybertruck, and the argument over whether it’s genius or a low-poly disaster has never really gone away.

The launch event set the tone for everything that followed. Tesla’s chief designer, Franz von Holzhausen, took a metal ball to the supposedly unbreakable windows, and they promptly shattered. Not exactly the show of strength Tesla was after, and a pretty cringe bit of live theatre for a truck sold on its toughness.

Then came the production delays, shifting specs, and a price that jumped from the original promises. Musk once talked about selling 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. According to Kelley Blue Book figures reported by Reuters, Tesla sold just 20,237 in the US during 2025, down 48% from the year before. Yikes.

We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s design misadventures since that first reveal, and it constantly surprised us for all the wrong reasons. We looked at early Cybertruck sketches that show how different the finished design could have been, and even imagined what happens when other carmakers go angular in our look at what every car would look like as a Cybertruck. The Mini Cooper, the first car I ever owned, in particular, wasn’t the looker it used to be.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

But the issues ran deeper than looks. In June 2023, we reported on leaked design and engineering flaws that made the Cybertruck sound even more terrifying, including problems with braking, handling, noise and water leaks. Then there’s the branding. In April 2024, we rounded up the six worst Cybertruck design fails, from that questionable logo to the accelerator pedal recall.

Then came the reports of bits falling off and the off-road truck getting stuck in mud – are you getting the picture? In March 2025, another Cybertruck design disaster emerged involving exterior panels coming loose. It’s quite something when a truck styled like an armoured tank can’t keep its own bodywork on.

To be fair, the Cybertruck was never meant to be universally loved, and ambition may have overtaken the practicalities of mass production. Musk wanted a vehicle that looked like nothing else on the road, and he got it. But good product design has to do more than turn heads. It has to work, make sense for the people buying it, and survive the rather less glamorous reality of everyday use, whether it's offroading or just driving to the shops without a bumper falling off. The Cybertruck struggled on all three counts.

That heavy, angular build also proved a barrier in Europe, where it failed to meet pedestrian-safety requirements. And the stainless-steel exterior may look suitably apocalyptic, but it brought its own manufacturing and finishing headaches.

Then there’s the branding. That huge angular silhouette was already shouting loud enough, and the aggressive typography and Cybertruck identity just pushed the whole thing further into concept-car territory. I love seeing designers take a big swing at something genuinely unusual. But there’s bold, and then there’s a design that seems to have skipped the bit where someone asks, ‘Is this actually a good idea?’

For contrast, check out some of the best car logos on the road today. Ferrari, Porsche and Mercedes have built enduring identities for a reason: they tell you something about the product and its heritage without yelling at you.

Tesla is now turning its attention to the Cybercab, its two-seat autonomous taxi, with the Texas factory being repurposed to ramp up production. The company is also pushing harder into AI and robotics, so the Cybertruck’s exit is part of a much bigger change of direction.

We’ve already had a glimpse of what that next chapter might look like, and Tesla’s Cybercab has its own rather silly design fail. Maybe the Cybertruck’s lessons haven’t quite sunk in yet.

So here’s to the end of the Cybertruck era, one that made us smile more than it had drivers, and to whatever the Cybercab era has in store.

#9094. Art Gallery of Ontario sets opening date for $73m new wing

Rendering of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery at the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto Courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time. Rendering courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time.

The Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO) in Toronto has announced that its new five-storey, C$100m ($73.4m), Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, which will display around 400 modern and contemporary works, will open to the public on 25 September 2027. The expansion project was first made public in April 2022.

“The Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery is more than an expansion project—it is Toronto and Canada announcing its global position,” Stephan Jost, the AGO’s outgoing director and chief executive, said in a statement. “When this gallery opens in September 2027, the world will be made aware of the strength of the AGO collection and the degree to which it has evolved to be truly global.”

The new building is the result of a collaboration between three architecture firms: the Toronto-headquartered firm Diamond Schmitt (known for its revamp of Emily Carr University of Art + Design in Vancouver and the forthcoming New Brunswick Museum in Saint John); the New York-based firm Selldorf Architects (of the recent renovations of the National Gallery in London and the Frick Collection in Manhattan); and Two Row Architect, headquartered in Ohsweken, Ontario (known for the Perry Centre for Native American Art at the Shelburne Museum in Vermont).

“It’s not a small project,” Jost said at the time of the launch in 2022. The 40,000-sq.-ft expansion, which overlooks downtown Toronto’s Grange Park, increases the AGO’s display space by around 30%, including 5,000 sq. ft of gallery spaces with 23ft-tall ceilings.

Rendering of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery at the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto Courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time. Rendering courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time.

The gallery is certainly in need of additional space for its collection of modern and contemporary work, which has grown by around 18,000 pieces in the past decade. In 2024 it received a gift of 37 works from the estate of the telecoms executive Philip B. Lind, including pieces by Laurie Simmons, Stan Douglas, Jeff Wall, Ai Weiwei, William Kentridge, Rodney Graham, Philip Guston and others. Last year, the gallery acquired more than 200 photographs by Peter Hujar and received more than 450 works from the late collectors Carol and Morton Rapp—among them works by Robert Rauschenberg, Claes Oldenburg, Kara Walker, Rachel Whiteread, Jasper Johns, Roy Lichtenstein, Lee Bontecoue, David Hockney and others. (The gallery also found itself at the centre of a culture war debate after opting not to acquire a work by the US photo-based artist and activist Nan Goldin.)

The AGO also boasts the largest public collection of Henry Moore’s work outside the UK—so much so that two years ago, to mark the 50th anniversary of the gallery’s Henry Moore Sculpture Centre, the city of Toronto declared 13 November to be Henry Moore Day.

The project of building a new wing was sparked by a lead gift of C$35m ($25.7m) from Dani Reiss, an art collector, chairman and chief executive of Canada Goose and member of the Order of Canada. The Reiss Gallery project is now fully funded, thanks to contributions from a community of supporters and the governments of Ontario and Canada.

Speaking on behalf of the federal government, Gregor Robertson, the minister of housing and infrastructure, said: “The federal government is proud to support this sustainable, state-of-the-art gallery that will host some of the world’s best modern and contemporary art for generations to come.”

The lion’s share of the donated pieces, from the late collectors Carol and Morton Rapp, are prints and photographs

Philip B. Lind left the Toronto museum a trove of works by Stan Douglas, Jeff Wall, Ai Weiwei, William Kentridge, Laurie Simmons and others

During Stephan Jost’s tenure, the leading art museum in Toronto has launched construction of a new contemporary art gallery, added more than 18,000 pieces to its collection and navigated plenty of drama

Construction of the 40,000 sq. ft space, dubbed the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, is expected to begin in early 2024, with an opening scheduled in 2027

Touch support and Spatial Preview will introduce new ways to create, sculpt and explore 3D work.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR has the best display our design editor has seen on a laptop. It also introduces touch input to an Apple laptop for the first time, and that could change how creatives interact with their software.

Maxon sees a world of potential, announcing that Cinema 4D and ZBrush, long-time features in our guides to best 3D modelling software and the best animation software, will get touch support for the new MacBook in late November. And that's not all. Cinema 4D is also getting a new capability that allows artists to preview 3D creations with Apple Vision Pro.

Maxon believes the new MacBook Pro will introduce an "entirely new dimension to professional creative workflows" with its tandem OLED display, intuitive touch capabilities, and powerful M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The touch display means artists will have new ways to explore interact directly with their 3D creations.

Whether building and animating complex 3D worlds in Cinema 4D or developing intricate digital sculptures in ZBrush, touch support is intended to bring the responsiveness of hands-on interaction to professional desktop workflows, complementing traditional mouse, keyboard, and trackpad workflows.

Maxon already has ZBrush for iPad, which made digital sculpting in the app more mobile and allowed artists to shape and refine their work with their fingers or Apple Pencil. Touch support on MacBook Pro extends that to the more familiar desktop experience.

While touchscreen displays on Windows laptops have been around for many years, Apple's PROLED XDR Display also delivers exceptional brightness, contrast, and color accuracy.

Meanwhile, upcoming Apple Vision Pro support for Cinema 4D will extend the creative process opening up collaborative, real-time three dimensional workflows. Through the new Spatial Preview API, artists using Mac Virtual Display on Apple Vision Pro will be able to explore, preview, and interact with Cinema 4D designs in immersive life-size detail, making it easier to evaluate proportions and composition before moving forward with production.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Rather than judging work based on a 2D image, artists and designers will be able to move through an interior, evaluate a proposed installation, or explore the layout of a space at real-world scale before anything is physically built. This could be particularly valuable for architectural visualisation, retail environments, exhibition spaces and experiential design.

The integration also aims to enable more seamless communication with clients and collaborators, allowing them to inhabit the same space at the same time, immersed in the scene or from a bird’s-eye view using Apple Vision Pro. For reviewers who may not be familiar with navigating 3D software, this could allow them to better understand the space, identify potential changes, and provide more informed feedback earlier in the creative process.

Cinema 4D and ZBrush will be immediately available on Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, which begins shipping 6 November, 2026. Touch support for Cinema 4D and ZBrush along with Open in Spatial Preview for Apple Vision Pro running visionOS 27 and Mac running macOS 27 will be available in late November.

A new Cinema 4D iPad app is also slated for release before the end of the year. You can learn more on the Maxon website.

#9091. Andy Warhol's Habibi Phase in Kuwait

Raed Yassin's exhibition “Warhol of Arabia” reimagines the pop artist's 1977 visit to the Gulf country and a bygone era in the Middle East.

VENICE — In January 1977, Andy Warhol skipped President Jimmy Carter’s inauguration to spend a week attending tea parties and dinners in Kuwait. He was invited by the country's national arts council and held a solo exhibition at the Salat Al Funoon gallery, featuring portraits of Mao Zedong and Marilyn Monroe and an array of flower prints. Domestically, his star was fading; with fewer patrons willing to meet his high asking prices, Warhol was under pressure to enter new markets. In Kuwait, where the recent oil boom had brought an influx of cash and a tether to the West and its cultural exports, he found more than a few interested buyers.

Nearly 50 years later, contemporary artist Raed Yassin has mounted a selection of photographic mixed-media works for the 61st Venice Biennale’s main exhibition, In Minor Keys, inventing scenes from that trip from the perspective of a fly on the wall.

“Warhol of Arabia” (all works 2016–2018) uses a real event as its anchor to paint a rich fiction using Pop aesthetics. In “The Party XII,” Warhol is depicted on the floor between a sheikh and a stylish kaftaned woman; Yassin painted only Warhol in color, making his hair pink and his glasses yellow, marking him as an outsider. “The Exhibition XIII” stamps four primary-colored headscarves onto a photo of Warhol with his Campbell’s soup can multiples, modifying the super-Western imagery the artist typically favored.

“The Gulf region in the 70s was kind of a black hole. No one knew what was going on, especially culturally,” Yassin told Hyperallergic. “You hear about oil and that kind of industry, but I was interested in what was beyond, what was happening in society. This is my imagination of it, which creates a different world entirely.”

An insult or tribute to the most-anticipated video game in history?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's under two weeks to go until the release of Grand Theft Auto VI for PS5 and Xbox, and the hype is approaching fever pitch. It was already the most-anticipated video game of all time. Now developer and publisher Rockstar Games is rolling out heavy digital and billboard advertising to cement the title's status as a global cultural event.

From Buenos Aires to Vienna, GTA VI ads have been appearing on the sides of buildings, at bus stops and in stadiums. At least one's already come in for a spot of artistic intervention after someone took advantage of game's visibility to make their own brand a household name, and it's sparked quite a debate.

The GTA 6 marketing has kicked off in more cities around the world: - Hamburg/Frankfurt/Leipzig, Germany 🇩🇪 - Buenos Aires, Argentina 🇦🇷 - London, UK 🇬🇧 - Paris, France 🇫🇷 - Singapore 🇸🇬 - Prague, Czech Republic 🇨🇿 - Taipei, Taiwan 🇹🇼 - Lisbon, Portugal 🇵🇹 - Santiago, Chile 🇨🇱 - Dubai, UAE 🇦🇪 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 🇧🇷 - Madrid, Spain 🇪🇸 The video also includes more footage from Cologne, Berlin, Munich, Vienna, Warsaw, São Paulo, New York, New Mexico, Tokyo, Osaka, Seoul, Hong Kong, Stockholm, Melbourne, Brisbane, Sydney, and Toronto. Enjoy!November 6, 2026

Sign painters Nick Birnie and Ian Potter spent over a week hand painting a huge GTA VI mural for Rockstar in Brooklyn, New York City. The artwork became an attraction, drawing fans who travelled to capture work in progress on the piece.

Within a month, the artwork had been tagged by a graffiti artist going by the name of Jelous, and the intervention has sparked quite a debate.

A post shared by jelous.ktd (@jelous.ktd)

Many people have expressed outrage at the desecration of the colossal tribute to Jason and Lucia from the upcoming game, with some saying the piece has been "ruined" by the graffiti artist.

"Hopefully they come and remove this crappy graffiti and fix the mural…. Also look on security cameras to find out where this guy lives and arrest him," one person writes on Instagram.

“As an Italian graffiti artist myself, I honestly think this is pretty disrespectful, even by graffiti standards,” someone writes over on Reddit.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

A post shared by Nick Birnie (@birntoutstudio)

But some think fans are being overly precious about what is, after all, a huge advert installed by a subsidiary of a $39.06 billion corporation that's using public space to push an $80-$100 game, even if the artwork was hand painted.

Others point out that crime is a central feature of the GTA franchise. Players can commit everything from minor traffic offences to first degree murder. Some think that makes the tag a fitting response.

"There's nothing more GTA than tagging a giant GTA mural," one person reckons. Some even suggest that Rockstar should add it to the game.

#9089. Only Known Manuscript of MLK's "I Have a Dream" Could Fetch $10M at Auction

The public will be able to view the handwritten final draft of the iconic speech at Christie's New York before it goes under the hammer in January.

The only handwritten manuscript of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s “I Have a Dream” speech, famously delivered on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial to 250,000 people on August 28, 1963, will be up for auction at Christie's on January 22, 2027.

Following a public week-long viewing in New York, the document is expected to fetch over $10 million at its single-lot sale. (Christie's did not publicly release an estimate.)

In the late 1990s, Xernona Clayton, a civil rights leader and pioneering broadcaster, discovered the papers in a desk drawer belonging to Edward T. Clayton, her late husband and one of Dr. King's speechwriters and close advisors.

Two years ago, she happened upon the manuscript again and worked with Christie's and her advisor, Eddie Bridgeman, to identify it as the only known handwritten final draft of the speech.

#9088. Holst completes Adjaye-designed mass-timber library in Oregon

Photography by Christian Columbres

US architecture studio Holst has created a mass-timber library in Oregon, with a series of tall columns at the entrance and a central atrium, after taking over the project from Adjaye Associates.

The East County Library in Gresham features a trapezoidal roof structure on top of a mostly square building envelope, creating multi-storey covered entry programmes on each side.

These entry programmes are lined with massive glued-laminated (glulam) mass-timber columns that Holst said speak to a primary effect of the design: “awe and accessibility”.

“One of our major main vision points of the project was this idea of awe and accessibility,” Holst principal and creative director Brittany Shreiner told Dezeen.

Shreiner said that the accessible component comes from the dual entry programmes that open up to a plaza on one side, with space taken from a converted street, and an elevated entryway on the other that features ramps.

A rail line is located on one side and a bus line on the other, connecting the building to the wider public realm.

For the team, the building needed to be a “big civic moment”, thus the massive columned entryway. However, Shreiner said that the awe the studio aspired to create was more akin to that of a forest, and the mass timber helped them to express that.

Structurally, the building has a mix of concrete and mass timber elements, with mostly wooden floorplates and some walls, and concrete-and-steel cores.

The facade is a mix of vertical timber elements interspaced with high-performance concrete bands with scalloped shapes and vertical bands of glass.

At one point, a grey-toned concrete panelling system marks the semi-circular protrusion where the structure’s amphitheatre is.

The appearance of the building is close to the original design submitted by Adjaye Associates – Holst was the architect of record at the start.

However, after misconduct allegations against Adjaye Associates founder David Adjaye were made public in a Financial Times investigation, the studio was released from this project, among others. Adjaye denies the allegations.

Shriener said that the biggest changes in the design were the removal of screens that were supposed to overhang from the covered entryways and a tower that extended past the roof plane.

“There was still a lot of design to be done [at that time], but the bones of the building were there. The community buy-in was there. The stakeholder buy-in was there,” said Shriener.

“So, the county was definitely clear in their intention that they did not want to proceed with Adjaye as part of our team, and that they basically trusted us to bring the project forward, but they didn’t want to see a total redesign by any means.”

Having recently solidified itself as a name in the US mass timber game with a tall building in Portland, the studio focused on optimising the timber usage as it took over the design. It worked closely with local mass-timber supplier TimberLab for the materials.

One detail that stands out is the notches in the timber columns and beams that give the structure a cabin-like or residential appearance, while remaining monumental in scale.

More than just a style conceit, the notches play a role in the ceiling plane, hiding the mechanical systems and lighting.

Inside, vestibules compress the entry to the library, which then opens up into a main core that runs between the entrances, with a double-height atrium space in the middle, complete with a wood-slatted spiral staircase.

For Shriener, this middle space represents a “clearing” in the forest.

The primary book-storage spaces surround the main central area, with smaller breakout rooms and classrooms lying mostly on the perimeter.

Mass-timber elements remain visible throughout the interior spaces, with green carpets at times continuing the forest metaphor.

On the roof, a series of sawtooth lightwells bring diffuse light into the main central space, while a rooftop patio allows guests to enjoy the views of the mountains beyond.

Elsewhere in Oregon, Holst created a Gaudí-informed apartment building wrapped in wood.

Other projects that were completed after the fallout from the Adjaye allegations include the Princeton Art Museum, where David Adjaye “stepped back” from the project in the late stages, according to Princeton.
