#9087. Six Stolen Picassos Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Home

Seven suspects were arrested in connection with the theft of the prints from L’Amandier restaurant in the south of France.

French authorities discovered six stolen Pablo Picasso prints under a pile of clothes in a home on the French Riviera on Tuesday, November 3, and arrested seven suspects for the theft, the French National Gendarmerie said in a press release. Details and images of the works have not yet been made public.

On the night of October 1, two masked intruders broke into L'Amandier, a restaurant in the village of Mougins, while a getaway driver remained on the lookout. The duo made away with six of the artworks on display in the restaurant's Salon Picasso lounge. The prints, which have an estimated worth of over €100,000 ($112,208), were reportedly found in perfect condition behind clothes and toolboxes in one of the village houses they searched, according to Le Monde.

Picasso first visited Mougins in 1936 and returned decades later to live out his last 12 years of life in Notre-Dame-de-Vie. L'Amandier's Salon Picasso lounge pays tribute to the Spanish artist and his impact on the former farming village, which became a tourism hotspot after his arrival.

6 standout designs that ruled the cinema screen this year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm calling it. 2026 is the year of the movie title card. Also known as intertitles, these stylised film openers have existed since the silent movie era, showcasing a unique and iconic artistic legacy that rivals some of the best movie posters.

Title cards aren't just for aesthetics; they offer a narrative anchor, a beat to collect yourself before the action begins. But of course, it's. not empty imagery. The best movie title cards can be a storytelling device in themselves, and this year we've seen some stunning examples.

In contrast to the film's bold poster typography featuring sturdy sans serifs and clean composition, The Bone Temple's title card feels surprisingly organic. Created in a natural, hand-drawn scrawl, the imperfection of the lettering gives it an almost juvenile feel.

Appearing just after a particularly violent opening, the silent serenity of the title card scene regrounds the audience, offering a moment of respite from the chaos. But set against the temple of bones, there remains an eeriness to the blood-red hue of the title card typography,

A post shared by Warner Bros. Philippines (@warnerbrosph)

Championing hand-crafted design, Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights took a delightfully strange approach to title card creation. Made using hair (including some of the lead actors' real locks!), the stop-motion title card is equal parts whimsical and slightly disturbing, setting the tone for the madness that ensues.

"We wanted it to feel completely human", Fennell explains in a behind-the-scenes sneak peek. "It's really thrilling to show the hands that make something," she adds. Wonderfully tactile and hauntingly beautiful, the title card demonstrates how thoughtful design can effortlessly set the tone of a film.

A prime example of how simple title cards can create a sense of tension, The Drama's erratic opening plants a seed of anxiety amid the intimacy of the dance scene. Using a jumbled mix of script fonts, stately serifs and bold sans serifs, the chaotic nature of the title card signals a sense of chaos amid the calm.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Appearing only fleetingly, almost as if the screen is glitching, the random fonts create a sense of visual disharmony as they flash across the scene. Appearing in a conventional white colour scheme, the juxtaposition of order and disarray builds a perfect layer of discomfort.

Obsession demonstrates one of my favourite movie tropes – the integrated title card. After a particularly harrowing scene, protagonist Bear is seen weeping on his bed as a tense score begins to creep in. The camera pans down to reveal the Obsession title card woven into the duvet.

The simple visual effortlessly creates an eerie effect, as the viewer is thrown into the film's suffocatingly bleak universe. Purposefully domestic in nature, the tactile title card hints that the horror is not abstract or far away, but lingering under our noses.

Wildwood's beautiful title card was created by hand, using tactile design to breathe life into each letter form. With diverse natural wood textures, crawling ivy and powered pigment details, each human-made design has its own story woven between the branches.

With animation studio Laika heavily promoting its human-made artistry, it's no surprise this dedicated craft extends to its stunning title card. Demonstrating the beauty that comes from intricate, time-intensive work, Wildwood's title card shines as a rejection of the increasing quantity of AI slop taking over cinema.

Resident Evil title card. https://t.co/ZxxvIHJlthNovember 2, 2026

The Resident Evil title card is perhaps one of the most controversial on the list for an unexpected reason. With the franchise's origins stemming from the gaming world, many die-hard fans were anticipating the game's iconic title voice narration, something that director Zach Cregger opted against.

The tense, thumping score, paired with the rapid warping of the bold title card, creates an eerie effect that stands strong on its own (basically, doing away with the campiness of the game narrator was a good move). Grungy and terrifying, the title card perfectly encapsulates the film's decay into raw, unrelenting horror.

#9085. Tatiana Bilbao creates rammed-earth installation at Art Omi

Mexico-based architecture practice Tatiana Bilbao Estudio has created a large-scale outdoor installation made of rammed earth derived from local soil that’s meant to break down over time for New York arts centre Art Omi.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio‘s Borrowed Earth installation consists of four 7.5-foot-tall rammed-earth cruciform crosses, with a shorter cross form in the centre that serves as a bench. Each form was made with compacted soil harvested from the Hudson Valley area.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio based the design around a “repeatable basic unit” that eventually became the bench and surrounding columns.

The Borrowed Earth piece was commissioned by arts centre Art Omi, which oversees a 120-acre sculpture park at its campus in Ghent, New York.

Art Omi curator Julia van den Hout said rammed earth can be a “challenging material”, and it shaped much of the project’s design.

“They were not always crosses in our initial conversations,” van den Hout told Dezeen.

“As we started getting into the reality of trying to figure out how to construct this – because rammed earth is a challenging material to work with – and thinking structurally about how this would be built up, during those conversations, [it] shifted to being a cruciform column.”

“It also really resonated [because] it has such a strong classic modernist shape.”

The Art Omi and Tatiana Bilbao Estudio teams constructed the columns on site with guidance from rammed-earth consultant Raíz Arquitectura studio based out of Mexico.

The team used soil from a construction site just down the road from Art Omi, according to van den Hout. They mixed it with sand and lime and then packed the mixture layer by layer into wooden formwork to create the sculptures.

Van den Hout says the installation is designed to decay over a period of about two years, although the team does not have “a strict answer” about how long it will last given external elements like weather.

“It’ll be an experiment,” she said. “We don’t quite know how fast it’s going to go. It is definitely soft. It crumbles. It’s lovely and tactile in that when you touch it, you really feel that sense that erosion can happen pretty easily. But simultaneously, they feel very stable.”

Recently, MOS Architects created a sculpture at Art Omi made of aluminium, while Young Projects installed a frayed, wooden pavilion at the park in 2024.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio completed a sprawling aquarium in 2023 in Mexico, where the studio is primarily based and also spoke to Dezeen in 2019 about the country’s rising generation of prominent female architects.

#9084. Wexner Center for the Arts to Keep Name Despite Founder’s Epstein Ties

Hundreds had urged Ohio State University to remove Les Wexner's name from campus buildings over his connections to Jeffrey Epstein.

Ohio State University (OSU) has called off the school's review process to consider removing billionaire benefactor Les Wexner's name from campus buildings, despite hundreds of renaming requests citing Wexner's connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Interim Provost Trevor Brown's decision, made public last Friday, November 6, overrides the advisory committee conducting the review.

It also comes as a blow to the university's Wexner Center for the Arts staff, who told Hyperallergic they've been “directly affected” by public discontent with the Center's association with Wexner.

“Workers will bear the brunt of this decision, fielding angry and hostile comments from the public and having the work we do questioned for its association with the Wexner name,” said a representative of the Wexner Center's staff union, Wex Workers United (WWU), in a statement. Wexner funded the art institution's creation and remains the center's board chair.

In June, the Wexner Center's Executive Director Cat Predmore told WOSU that one artist and one grantmaking organization have withdrawn from showing art at and funding the Center, respectively, over Wexner's connections to Epstein.

#9083. Getty to help conserve art-filled 17th-century church in Peruvian Andes

Members of the local community in the Church of Rondocan Photo: Alejandra Velez, © 2026 J. Paul Getty Trust

An art-filled 17th-century church in the Andes mountains will soon begin five years of conservation work. The project will strengthen the building and preserve its collection of 330 historical objects—including eight paintings by the artist Bernardo Bitti (1548-1610), an Italian Jesuit priest who introduced Mannerism to the Viceroyalty of Peru in the 16th century.

Getty will work with the Peruvian Ministry of Culture to conserve the Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, also known as the Church of Rondocan—named for the town in the Cusco region where it was built. The project will include seismic stabilisation using local materials; located 3,400m above sea level, the 340-sq.-m church is in an area prone to earthquakes.

“We provide all the advanced conservation techniques available, and we handle the structural design of the project,” Claudia Cancino, a principal project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute (GCI), tells The Art Newspaper. The Peruvian government will finance the work, which will cost $5m and start in 2027. Like other churches in the Andean highlands, Rondocan has adobe walls (1.2m thick), buttresses and a wooden truss roof.

“The project is not only about the temple and its walls. It’s about the cultural and spiritual heritage of the church,” says César Ccorimanya Mayta, the parish priest at Rondocan for the past 17 years.

The Church of Rondocan and its surrounding landscape Photo: Luigi Barazzetti © 2026 J. Paul Getty Trust

Involving the community as caretakers of the temple is part of the conservation process. Cancino and her team completed a similar project at the Church of Santiago Apóstol in the nearby town of Kuñotambo in 2019. As part of that initiative, they showed locals how best to take care of the building—including deceptively simple tasks, like cleaning the floors.

“You have to understand how to sweep the church and with what, because if you stir up too much dust it sticks to the murals,” Cancino says. “All this training was done with the community of Kuñotambo. We even have a manual in Quechua,” the local Indigenous language.

Through the work in Kuñotambo, the GCI became familiar with the Church of Rondocan. “The community asked for our support so that they could request the Archdiocese of Cusco and the Ministry of Culture to work on their church,” Cancino says.

Technical examination and assessment of a painting from the series Principales Misterios de la Vida y Muerte de Cristo Nuestro Salvador y la Virgen Santísima, attributed to Bernardo Bitti © 2024 J. Paul Getty Trust

“This church is much more than a historic building. It is part of the community’s memory, identity and everyday life,” Fernando López Sánchez, Peru’s vice minister of cultural heritage, said in a statement.

As part of the conservation project, a Bitti painting will travel to Los Angeles for scientific analysis and conservation on the Getty campus.

Bitti arrived in Peru in 1575, creating paintings for churches in Lima and Cusco. When the Jesuits were expelled from the Americas by the Spanish Crown in 1767, their works were sold. It is believed that the parish priest at Rondocan at that time bought Bitti’s paintings in Cusco and had them transferred to the church. The discovery, less than two decades ago, of the only complete series of eight Bitti canvases has sparked renewed interest in the study of his work.

In addition to the paintings, the church’s collection includes sculptures from the viceroyalty era, manuscripts and silver liturgical objects. “The art collection in this small town in the middle of nowhere is breathtaking,” Cancino says.

#9082. The Zen Mona Lisa

A review of an ancient Chinese ink painting takes an art critic on a journey through his own past.

Every summer Jonah compiled a list of about a hundred upcoming museum shows for the newspaper’s special fall preview section. The first time he did it they were visiting Nadia’s college friend at her parents’ house in Pasadena, where he had to share a queen-size bed with Nadia and eight-month-old Orly. Fording hundreds of press releases, making decisions, and writing one-to-two-sentence synopses of complex shows he hadn’t seen while exhausted and sleepless was a trial. But the next year found him more confident, and ultimately the process became so automatic that it made no impression on him at all. If someone asked him in August, after he had filed his piece, what fall shows he was looking forward to, he would have to refer back to the document to come up with an answer.

One exhibit that did stick in his mind, though, the year Orly was six, was of a famous Chinese ink painting, a still life of persimmons, making a brief visit to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. It would be coming from the Japanese monastery which had acquired it when it was already nearly 300 years old and which had then kept it mostly rolled up and hidden away since the early 1500s. Jonah mentioned the show to his editor as one he’d like to cover, emphasising how unprecedented it was for the piece to travel and reminding her that he was her only freelancer with any affinity for, or knowledge of, Asian art.

She was amenable to his writing about it, she told him, but said that, because of the expense of covering the war in Ukraine, the art section had no travel budget left for the year.

“Do you really have to see it in person?” she asked.

Then cannily, or guilelessly, he added that he planned to go see it regardless. He figured that after more than a decade as an art critic, it was time to admit that art was important to him, and that so long as she did pay him to write something, he would at least break even on the experience. She offered to pay for a night in a hotel and he replied that he was planning to stay with his cousin.

“Well,” she said noncommittally, “see if you can find a cheap flight.”

Using credit card points, he found one for a couple of hundred dollars. He checked with his cousin and made plans to stay for two nights; it would be the longest he had been alone since Orly was born. Then he forgot about it, mostly. But he would mention his upcoming trip now and then to this or that person, amused to cut the figure of an adult whose job let him travel. Downtown to take notes about a conceptual art show, he met his father for coffee.

“Wow!” Alan exclaimed when Jonah told him about the ink painting. “I always wanted to see that but your mother and I were never in Kyoto on the right day.”

When the time came to go and Jonah found himself alone with a backpack on the E train, bound for Kennedy Airport, he was bemused again. As a younger man, he had travelled to escape his ordinary life, to fling himself without boundaries into unfamiliar locales. His last visit to San Francisco had been to visit a girl he’d briefly dated in New York, and he could still summon up the Pacific smell of the air when he first stepped out of the airport, the dark luxury of the apartment she was borrowing, the softness of her freckled, paper-white skin as they made love and fell asleep in a narrow guest-room bed. She had reminded him of a doe. Now, as he passed through the airport security line in New York, endured a two-hour delay caused by San Francisco air traffic related to the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference, read the London Review of Books, crammed himself into an economy seat, watched half a movie on his iPad, and took a cab, at his cousin’s suggestion, to Bernal Heights, it all felt more like an errand, albeit a pleasant one, than an adventure. The air smelled of nothing. His own company felt like a childhood friend he was glad to see again, but with whom, because it had been so long, he felt shy.

First thing the following morning, Jonah accompanied his cousin, an accomplished video game designer, as he walked his dog in a nearby park. They hadn’t met in years, and Jonah felt shy with him, too — as well as rebuked in his own aimless financial irresponsibility by the cousin’s comfortably furnished 3-bedroom house with basement rental apartment attached. Looking for something to talk about, he asked whether there had been many protests about Israel’s response to the attacks of October 7.

“Not really,” his cousin said. “I did drive past one group of people with signs that said ‘Stop the Genocide.’”

His tone made clear what he thought of the protestors’ use of the word “genocide.” Not seeing any benefit in starting an argument with his host at 7:30 in the morning, Jonah changed the subject. He went and climbed a nearby hill for its view of the city; returned to the house, where his cousin fed him breakfast; and rode the bus to a still awakening Chinatown to see a show someone had told him about, work by an artist he liked at a gallery he had encountered at art fairs but never visited in person. He chatted with the young man behind the desk, asking what else there was to see in the neighbourhood and sharing his concern that the artist, a Native American ceramicist who had gotten very popular, might get boxed into grinding out the same thing over and over. Because the young man asked, Jonah also shared his name. There was a photography gallery a few blocks away, another one Jonah knew by reputation; walking there he saw a large protest of the summit that had delayed his flight.

He got past the desk and into the show — tasteful, boring photography by a successful Japanese artist, what he privately thought of as “rich people art” — with only a brief hello, but then turned around, just when he would have walked out again, to see that the gallery founder and two directors had emerged to greet him.

“They told us you were coming,” explained one of the directors, a pretty young woman in a severe business suit. Once the founder had shaken his hand and gone back to his office, Jonah let the pretty young director show him around the exhibit he’d already dismissed as well as the gallery’s back office and viewing room. He took his usual approach in such situations, making small talk as if at a cocktail party and biding his time. He admired the unique design of the display racks in the viewing room. He inquired after her family and asked where she liked to eat in the neighbourhood. As soon as he could he slipped out and hurried over to City Lights, where he bought two paperbacks by the Sicilian writer Leonardo Sciascia, whom he’d never read before.

The restaurant she recommended turned out to be an ornate Szechuan spot, deserted at that hour, whose prices he could not possibly afford. Slinking out again after looking at the menu he felt foolish to have expected anything else. Fortunately he’d overheard the clerk at City Lights mention another place, an old-school Hunanese lunch counter where there was a television playing the local news and they did not offend Jonah’s sensibilities by charging for tea. Later he rode out to the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive to see the exhibition of a grad school friend, another conceptual artist who made work about North American settler colonialism; the next morning, he visited a sculptor who had gone to college with Nadia and had just spent six months carving the impurities out of an enormous chunk of quartz salvaged from a commercial rock quarry.

This sculptor’s New York gallery had just closed and he had a new baby in a carrier on his chest. Jonah’s heart was in his mouth every time the sculptor leaned over his opus, bringing the baby’s head within an inch of a corner; he remembered the dirty looks he used to get from old women in Jackson Heights when they saw him carrying his own newborn infant under one arm like a football. He and the sculptor went out for dim sum and to a bookstore and the sculptor shared the advice another artist had given him about making money.

“‘Use archival material,’” he said, “‘and get used to doing the same thing over and over.’”

Then Jonah walked a mile and a half to the Asian Art Museum, which had been closed to the public to host a grand lunch for the spouses of the heads of state in town for APEC.

“Jill Biden was standing right here two hours ago,” the museum’s press chief told him, grinning and squeezing his arm, once he’d gotten past security and been led into the dim and empty gallery. “I’ll leave you alone.”

Publicists liked to talk, and curators liked to lecture, but Jonah had learned to be forthright about his need for solitude. This time they had agreed ahead of time that he would have 45 minutes to himself before the curator arrived to explain what he was supposed to think of the painting. When he was starting out, he had sometimes spent many hours over multiple days confronting a work that perplexed him. In this case, having already seen many images of what turned out to be a very easily photographed black and white art work, and having already begun to write down ideas earlier in the day, he could probably have made do with a glance. He was unlikely to experience any transcendence in such a tightly choreographed encounter, anyway. He was just too contrary. But showing up felt like a matter of principle, and after all, it couldn’t hurt.

When the press contact, a former dancer type who later surprised Jonah by mentioning his wife and two children, returned with the curator, a trim older woman in an embroidered jacket, Jonah prepared to joust. She was perfectly nice and had interesting things to say. But he needed her to understand that he was no mere journalist, to whom the Zen esthetic was news, while she, as an academic, had to demonstrate her mastery of the material. Once he felt they had both made their points, he looked at his watch, and they continued next door to a Japanese pop art exhibit. Then the curator excused herself, but the former dancer offered Jonah a tour of the rest of the museum, and Jonah couldn’t see how to refuse, even though his feet hurt and his eyes were exhausted. He hadn’t ever been there before and, as the dancer pointed out, there was no way of knowing if he’d ever be back.

When finally he left, with many thanks and professions of good will, he got on a train to a gentrified section of Oakland for dinner with a close college friend who had, after an interval in academia, become a corporate lawyer. Jonah held the friend’s new baby and then, leaving the baby and his older brother with either the night nurse or the mother in law — she wasn’t introduced — he, his friend, and his friend’s wife, also a corporate lawyer, walked to a nearby French restaurant. Jonah had been surprised, because his friend always seemed worried about money, by how nice his house was, but he supposed it made sense. The first thing his friend said, once they had been seated and had ordered some appetizers, was, “Flying across the country to see one painting is completely ridiculous.”

Jonah wasn’t sure whether he was meant to litigate this question, for entertainment’s sake, or to agree that he had wandered into an unbelievable life. He suspected the latter, but either way he didn’t feel up to it.

“Well,” he said mildly, “art is important to some people.”

“No, of course,” his friend replied, and Jonah stopped listening. In the morning he discovered that a train ran directly to the airport from quite close to his cousin’s house. There had been no reason to take a cab when he arrived. He began transcribing his notes on the airplane, and then began writing, and when this flight, too, was delayed, and they were all forced to deplane for several hours, he was delighted. The airline gave them food vouchers,  there was a decent enough sushi counter, and this way he could finish his piece and finish watching Parasite on his iPad before returning to family life. It was a beautiful experience. He was engaged in what he was doing, but with something deeper than his anxious ordinary mind; he could feel himself pirouette around the ink painting’s formal qualities and Buddhist subtext like an ice skater. “The point of this minimalism isn’t to make anything simple,” he concluded, after about 1000 words, “but to cut away distractions and reveal how complicated the world actually is.”

He filed that evening from Kennedy Airport, and when there was no reply the following day, he wondered if he should call. But then the assistant art editor sent an edit, and he dared hope he could get through the whole process without talking on the phone at all. He did end up speaking to the assistant editor, because she would need a synopsis of his piece for a meeting the following week and called to ask him to write one for her. In the course of their exchange, he mentioned that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa.” She suggested putting this phrase in the subheadline, and to make this intelligible, he agreed to add the fact that some people called “Six Persimmons” the “Zen Mona Lisa” to his story.

When the piece was published, he got vastly more response than he usually did, which is to say that as many as three or four people emailed him about it. One was a former college professor, who said that he wasn’t sure either of them had brought their best to the class they had shared, but that he congratulated Jonah on conserving his energies for such top-flight art writing. The next week Jonah went to Chinatown to visit an artist he might profile for a museum catalogue, a renowned older Japanese woman who had lived like a squatter in an unfurnished loft for 40 years. The gallerist who would be paying him for this, if she decided to spend what he was asking, sat between them as they chatted, interrupting their rapport from time to time to underline the parts of the artist’s life that she felt were important art historically. When she got up to use the bathroom, the artist followed her with her eyes.

“She’s okay,” the artist said. “But I think something weird about her. Like whenever we travel, she insist on getting one room with king size bed.”

On his way to Tribeca, where he was meeting his father for coffee, Jonah ran into a different art dealer, the one whose conceptual art show he had just reviewed, and she invited him into her office for a chat. They talked about marriage and their children, as they usually did, and she thanked him for the review, which he shrugged off.

She had worked at a mega gallery before opening her own space, and she told him that reviews in his paper had been the only ones the mega gallerist cared about. They appeared in sales presentations. They played a key role in what she called the mega gallerist’s “ongoing pissing contest” with his peers.

“Yeah,” Jonah laughed, “and then I get $250.”

The dealer’s jaw dropped, and he in turn stared right back at her. He couldn’t remember having ever surprised her before.

“Yeah,” he repeated. “Two-fifty for the short ones.”

“But you have so much power!” she exclaimed.

“How was the piece?” Alan asked him, once they were sitting side by side in the little cafe that now occupied the former boarding house where Frederick Douglass had first slept when he came to New York.

“To be honest,” Jonah said, “I think it comes through pretty well in reproduction.” He made a deprecating gesture. “You know, it’s black and white.”

“Oh, yeah, no,” Jonah said, “it was a great trip. I’m glad I went.”

He walked Alan back to the loft and went upstairs to say hello to his mother, to whom he couldn’t help boasting that he’d gotten some nice emails about his latest review.

“Oh, I’m so glad!” she exclaimed. “Because I saw someone on Facebook making fun of you for calling it the Zen Mona Lisa.”

Crafting a logo for a sports tournament is no easy job. It has to appeal to sports fans, who are notoriously conservative. It's going to have to work at tiny sizes, on a phone screen, and at massive sizes like a billboard or a stadium banner. The best sports logos manage all of the above.

It also has to make its point quickly and efficiently, because ordinary (non-designer) people are barely going to give it a second glance. So it usually pays to make the central visual idea blindingly obvious.

With this in mind, when I first saw the logo for the 2027 FIVB Men’s Volleyball World Cup, my reaction was: "Er… what that's supposed to be exactly?

Representing the tournament taking place in Poland next September, the logo emblem is a tall white shape with spikes at the top, a cluster of small squares in the middle and wavy stripes flaring out towards the base.

Perhaps I'm missing something, not being a volleyball fan myself. But to my eyes, it didn't look like... anything.

According to the press release, the inspiration was the World Cup trophy, whose “industrial form” has been distilled into a minimalist mark. And sure enough, when you look at the very distinctive trophy, it does look a lot like it. But it's not a pure representation, and that's deliberate.

Instead, four ideas are said to come together in the logo: the silhouette of the trophy, a circle representing the Earth, a sweeping curve representing the net, and reaching hands and a rising ball for the players. In the press release Maciej Bogusz, marketing director for the local organising committee, also added a fifth: the fans, represented by a wave rippling through the base.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Once you stare at the logo for a bit and pick out all these elements, yep, they're all present and correct. But that's kind of the problem: you have to stare to pick them out. All these concepts don't just magically mesh into one simple design; indeed, there are so many, that feels like it'd be close to impossible.

At the same time, it annoys the heck out of me when people judge a logo on first sight, because that's not how a logo should be judged. A logo is not primarily designed to be liked on first sight, it's designed to work over time.

The history of design is littered with logos that attracted a wave of negativity on first release, yet ended up being loved over time. And I don't want to make the same mistake here.

A post shared by Polska Siatkówka (@polskasiatkowka_official)

So here's something positive I can say: this doesn’t look like any other sports logo I can think of. There’s no generic shield, no generic ball with a swoosh, no cliches of any kind really.

Remember the London 2012 logo? It was widely ridiculed at first, but by the time the Olympic Games started, it had become a welcome part of the furniture.

This design now has plenty of time to do the same. Its first big outing is on 3 December, when the draw will take place 125m underground in the Wieliczka Salt Mine (because why not, eh?). And when the games start in Kraków, seven months later, the shape that looks so wrong to me may look, well, entirely right.

Honestly, I’m not convinced yet. But ask me again in September. My answer may be very different.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9080. Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?

From Willem de Kooning’s miserable nudes to Alexandra Barth’s hot and bothered architecture, sex is in the air in Chicago.

CHICAGO — I see a lot of exhibitions in Chicago, and lately, I have been noticing more than a few that feel almost ridiculously erotic. I mean, I get it, there's always been plenty of eros in art, but I haven't observed it much lately at the school where I teach nor in the shows that I view. Is sex back? Or it could just be me. I turned 50 this past year, and popular culture suggests that this might be what happens around my age, à la Sharon Horgan's Youth and Olivia Colman's Wicker, both recent screen-based explorations of lusty midlife ladyhood.

For those who have never had one or maybe never will, female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100. It is not an easy ride. Shifting from one state to the other causes severe whiplash for driver and passengers alike. That’s based on an admittedly minuscule survey, though fear not, this will not be a personal essay about my own sexuality or that of my acquaintances. God, no. Maybe after everyone’s dead. What proceeds, instead, is a round-up of exhibitions that, for me, have a strong connecting thread, obviously red, and not discussed much if at all in the various associated didactics.

What shows? Last spring, Alice Tippit’s sly, meticulous paintings at the DePaul Art Museum had me thinking I probably needed to start talking to a therapist again, because what was going on in my head was not articulated anywhere in the otherwise delightful catalogue. Not even close. During the summer, SHADOW at tête-à-tête-à-tête, a wicked little curatorial project of Shannon Stratton, included Holly Murkerson’s sensuous photographs of a stone passageway worth entering and two dark leather-and-wood stools by David Sprecher and Neiva Mulhearn that required straddling and peering into.

What wasn’t a turn-on was the Art Institute of Chicago’s summer blockbuster, Willem de Kooning Drawing. You wouldn’t know from the glowing reviews or polite museum text that miserable naked women filled the walls. I like a good nude as much as anyone, but at some point, maybe it was the third room — definitely by the time I got to the giant rowboat charcoals of the mid-60s — de Kooning’s subjects started to look like crime victims.

Left: Lee Miller, “Woman with Hand on Head” (also known as “Coiffure”) (1931), photograph; right: Lee Miller, “Charlie Chaplin with chandelier" (1932), photograph (both photos courtesy Art Institute of Chicago)

It's the time of year when the IRS and state tax agencies send out notices for additional taxes, missed payments, and other tax issues.

If you've ever received one, you've probably noticed that the amount due can have three components: tax, interest, and penalties.

#9078. Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge

The Met Museum’s “Chasing Clouds” is a pleasing romp through the technical problem of capturing clouds at photography’s beginning.

The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are so ubiquitous that it’s hard to believe they once presented one of photography’s greatest technological challenges. The Met exhibition Chasing Clouds is a pleasing romp through the history of this problem through a union of art and science, spanning the early 1800s to 1929 — roughly photography’s first century. While the medium showed promise as “the pencil of nature,” its first processes were overly sensitive to blue light, registering the sky as a blank white space, impossibly overexposed.

While this lent some images a minimalist mystique, like John Beasley Greene’s “The Nile in Front of the Theban Hills” (1853–54), other photographers resorted to painting clouds into their landscapes by hand. An initial breakthrough came when French photographer Gustave Le Gray figured out how to stitch together two pictures — one calibrated to sky, and the other to land and sea. (Photographic fakery is as old as the medium itself.)

Though the exhibition begins with painted cloud studies and ends with photographic modernism, visual discoveries unfold in a dialogue between painting and technology rather than as a scientific march from one to the other. This makes for a much more interesting story; obsolescence is often a capitalist public relations trick.

#9077. "Direct and unrefined" materials create tactile interior at Jeju restaurant by &Daughters

Canadian studio &Daughters used basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood to design Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver that features traditional touches in a contemporary interior.

The architect’s starting point for the design was the restaurant’s menu, which includes modern dishes developed by chef Dylan Kim, traditional dishes created by his mother, chef Myungseok “Julie” Suh and dishes that they created together.

“The restaurant exists in the space where these two narratives meet,” &Daughters principal Emma Sims told Dezeen.

“We began to think of tradition and reinterpretation as the foundation for the design, translating this relationship into a physical space through a specific set of people, places, materials and traditions.”

While Jeju’s exterior has a modern steel-mesh facade, the interior juxtaposes wood and concrete for a warmer, more tactile feel.

At the heart of the 44-seat restaurant is a reinterpretation of a traditional thatched house from Jeju Island, South Korea, called a chogajip.

This was constructed using lumber and hand-thatched grass, and creates an artisanal focal point for the space.

Other materials, including basalt, were chosen by &Daughters for Jeju to ensure a natural feel.

Basalt was used for the bar, chef’s table and host stand, while cork cladding helps create a soft feel while adding acoustic dampening.

The studio kept the existing concrete floor but polished it to reveal variations in its colour.

“The palette is quite simple – basalt, cork, raw concrete masonry units, polished concrete, wood and thatch,” Sims said.

“Basalt is one of the most recognisable materials of Jeju Island,” she continued.

“Formed through volcanic activity, it is found throughout the island’s landscape, architecture and traditional stone walls. Beyond that, we were interested in materials that felt direct and unrefined, allowing them to retain their natural character.”

The studio wanted to “introduce elements of tradition, ritual and memory into the interior,” Sims said.

As well as the thatched house, another traditional architectural feature from Jeju, a jeongnang three-pole gate, was also introduced to the interior.

“Historically used as a means of communicating whether a household was home, away or nearby, it offered an alternative to a conventional locked entrance, rooted in trust and shared understanding,” Sims said.

“At Jeju, we incorporated our interpretation into the glazing beside the entrance, where staff lower two poles each day to signal that the restaurant is open and guests are welcome, raising them again at the end of service,” she continued.

“In this way, a traditional architectural element becomes an active part of the restaurant’s daily life.”

Other restaurants recently featured on Dezeen include a brick-clad eatery in London’s Soho area and a bistro in Montreal influenced by Japanese metabolism.

#9076. Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallegic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).

When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.

That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives, you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?

Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”

MC: And my editor was like, “Yeah, you can't do that. No one's gonna want to read a book that you wrote simply for money.” But I also knew that this was a commercial idea, and that did inform it. I have been quite shameless about the fact that I want my work to reach a wide audience. That has always, always mattered to me. It was the beginning of the pandemic, and part of the way that I pitched it was this idea that there's gonna be a big financial crisis and the dynamics are more nuanced than simply talking about the one percent. There's this idea of a coming economic collapse or a coming financial crisis. But as soon as we're in it, it's not this cyclical model. The crisis is the system that we're in that is so broken.

H: That gradation of class that usually doesn't get talked about is such a crucial contribution of this book. What led you to stratify these stories based on subcategories that often just get collapsed into “working class, middle class, upper class”?

MC: Class is really informative about who I am and how I move through the world and my relationships. And I felt like it was really, really lacking in our discourse. I feel a bit hesitant to use the word “discourse,” but it's just true. And it's not just about discourse, it's more mundane than that. It's the way that someone like me can say, “I'm an Arab, cis, heterosexual woman,” with total ease, but class doesn't really come into it. There's a dishonesty there. Actually, class is really, really important. And many of us aren't really talking about that in accurate and fruitful ways.

They said they wouldn't do it. A touchscreen MacBook has been rumoured since the dawn of time (well, the noughties), but, in a quote that's been infinitely dredged up across the internet over the last couple of weeks, Steve Jobs himself decried the concept as "ergonomically terrible". But Jobs also famously asked, "Who wants a stylus?" And the answer among millions of Apple Pencil users seems to be a resounding, "Us!"

And after a few days with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I'm happy to report that this is very much a device—perhaps even the ultimate device—for creatives. But rather than the ability to touch the screen, it's all about the quality of that 'PROLED' display itself. Turns out there's a reason Apple decided to lead with that, and not touch, in the name of the device.

Simply put, it's the best laptop screen I've ever seen. With up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast, and P3 + Adobe RGB colour, this is a best-in-class display that puts every other OLED laptop screen I've used to shame. It gives creatives a portable reference-quality display, which means it recreates video, colour and contrast as faithfully as possible. Once you've used the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, everything else looks washed-out in comparison, and for that reason alone it's impossible not to recommend for creatives – so long as the small matter of the $2,899 starting price isn't a barrier.

When it comes to touch, as I've written before, in my testing I've found it to be a nice-to-have rather than a need-to-have. Now that we're all touchscreen natives (which wasn't so much the case when Jobs made those comments in 2010), certain navigational actions just feel right, even on a laptop. Scrolling through windows, pinching to zoom in on a photo or map, scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro; there are plenty of times when touching the screen feels more intuitive than reaching for the trackpad. And Apple's subtle UI tweaks, such as having navigational icons expand when touched, make the whole thing feel more natural.

But equally, there were plenty of times when I preferred to use the trackpad – particularly when a certain level of accuracy was required. And despite Apple claiming to have produced a newly designed hinge with greater stability, it still wobbles. There's just no getting around the fact that a touchscreen on a vertical display is less ergonomic than it is on a flat one.

From a design perspective, the new MacBook Pro isn't a game-changer – unless you really missed the illuminating Apple logo (another noughties mainstay). There are improvements here and there; the Dynamic Island takes up less space than the notch, and slightly smaller bezels result in slightly larger viewing areas. But perhaps the most meaningful design change is the reduction in weight. That OLED panel has allowed for a 14% weight loss – making the 14-inch model, somewhat ironically, lighter than the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air.

But everything pales next to the screen. The PROLED XDR looks incredible. If you're looking for the most impressive visual fidelity available on a laptop, here it is. You can touch it if you like.

I’ve tested a fair few drawing tablets over the years, and while the iPad is still the default for many digital artists, Wacom is clearly keen to lure creatives away. The MovinkPad 11 is one of its more interesting attempts, and this deal is a good excuse to take a look.

Wacom is selling the MovinkPad 11 with a case for £402.70 with the code CASE20 at checkout. That’s down from £469.96, a saving of £67.26 (around 14%). The tablet alone is listed at a discounted £429.98, so you’re paying less for the tablet and case together than for the tablet by itself. It’s a handy extra, too, on a tablet that’s made to be tossed in a bag and used anywhere.

The MovinkPad 11 is built around the Pro Pen 3, not a generic Android slate with stylus support bolted on. The 11.45-inch display has a 2200 x 1440 resolution and a 90Hz refresh rate, and the screen is etched glass. If you’ve ever drawn on the slick glass of a regular tablet, you’ll know it can feel like sketching on a bathroom mirror. The textured surface adds a little grip and feels much closer to paper.

The Pro Pen 3 offers 8,192 levels of pressure sensitivity and 60-degree tilt recognition, and it needs no battery or charging. Those numbers look good on a spec sheet, but what I notice more is how naturally it responds to light pressure and follows your strokes.

It runs Android 14 with 8GB RAM and 128GB storage, so you don’t need a computer. You can download drawing apps such as Clip Studio Paint, and Wacom includes a two-year Clip Studio Paint DEBUT licence.

It isn’t the most powerful Android tablet around, and the screen suits sketching and illustration better than big professional workflows, but for that exact art need, it's a better choice than an iPad Air. It’s a portable digital sketchbook, and at £402.70 with the case, it’s easy to recommend.

Wacom’s premium MovinkPad Pro 14 is now 14% off too, and with its protective cover, it's a similar deal, saving £140.05. As my MovinkPad Pro 14 review found, its gorgeous OLED screen and Pro Pen 3 make it a serious iPad alternative.

#9073. The Big Review: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ★★★★½

“The Met’s prize Jackon Pollock”, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950), flanked by a pair of Lee Krasner’s collage paintings, Blue Level (1955, left) and Stretched Yellow (1955) Photo: Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy Metropolitan Museum of Art

He was Jack the Dripper. She was The Wife. That is how it went for artist couples in gender-coded mid-century America (and elsewhere). Yet, Lee Krasner (1908-84) played more than a supporting role in her decade-long marriage to Jackson Pollock (1912-56). When his work eclipsed hers, she remained as committed to her own painting as she was to every aspect of his life—except his infidelity and the alcoholism that in 1956 drove him to his death. Even then, she put her devotion to consequential use in securing his legacy. Now the time has come to fully appreciate hers.

That is the organising principle behind Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, the gorgeous and largely convincing blockbuster at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. While other US museums have previously surveyed the artists separately and in tandem, for the Met curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, none gave Krasner, a first-generation Abstract Expressionist, a fair shake.

Their exhibition strives to give a primacy to Krasner’s work that parallels Pollock’s. Note whose name comes first in the show’s title. Its subtitle likewise derives from a Krasner at the she-who-laughs-last finale. What’s more, a dramatically lit, black box of a gallery starts it off with a bracing presentation of six vertical abstractions that Krasner made in the 1950s by collaging cuttings from her unsold paintings with pieces of canvas and bits of Pollock’s drawings punctuated by slashes of pink and orange.

Nonetheless, the eye keeps moving to a window-like opening that functions as a proscenium for the theatre of Pollock’s Convergence: No. 10 (1952), an immense and riveting painting of black paint skeins shot with explosions of colour. Mounted on an angled, freestanding wall in another room, the sight offers viewers a taste of what is in store: signature Pollocks ricocheting off shape-shifting Krasners, and vice-versa.

If only the curators did not show Krasner still riding his coattails. Pollock’s name remains the bigger draw. Ultimately, he still comes off as the bigger trailblazer, and she, his foremost champion, more willing to risk failure to experiment and invent. As Breslin speculated during the press preview: “I don’t think we would have a Jackson Pollock if it weren’t for what Krasner did to support his work.”

There is no way to test that theory, but if Krasner and Pollock proves anything, it is that the artists’ relationship was so codependent that the reverse may be just as true. Yet, today her influence and market value pale before his. Krasner’s auction record, set at Sotheby’s in 2019, is $11.7m for The Eye is the First Circle (1960), one of her larger canvases in the show. That is not chump change, but this year Christie’s sold Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) for $181.2m, an eye-watering price but still short of the reported $200m that financier Ken Griffin paid David Geffen, in 2016, for Number 17A (also 1948).

Photo by Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy of The Met

Krasner and Pollock met in 1942, when she was better-known to the Abstract Expressionist crowd in New York and Pollock the only unfamiliar name in a show of American and European Modernists (partially recreated at the Met) that the painter John Graham organised and included works by both. By linking their small, vibrant abstractions with works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Henri Matisse, Amadeo Modigliani, Giorgio de Chirico and Willem de Kooning, the show virtually jumpstarted their careers. It also made them a couple.

Krasner introduced herself in a spontaneous visit to Pollock’s studio and was so dazzled that she hit a creative block. That did not stop them from dating. He was a Midwestern former student of Thomas Hart Benton in thrall to Picasso and Mexican muralists. She was inspired by Arshile Gorky’s abstractions and Matisse’s cut-outs. Soon he was importing a Matissean palette to his painting and showing at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of this Century gallery. Sales were not brisk. Pollock’s drinking was more prodigious. Krasner insisted they marry and move to Springs, in East Hampton—to protect him from himself—and persuaded Guggenheim to cover the downpayment.

Relocating did the trick for three unusually sober years—long enough for Pollock to produce his breakthrough drip paintings and achieve lasting fame, before settling, intermittently, into new bouts of alcoholism and depression; a creative paralysis set in. Krasner’s career took off, with a confident 1955 solo show at New York’s Stable Gallery.

Breslin and Kumar take care not to place the artists’ works close together, so Krasner’s modestly-scaled paintings can hook the eye without being overwhelmed by Pollock’s volatile monumentalism. Until she was widowed and took over Pollock’s now-famous barn, Krasner worked in their kitchen and he in an upstairs bedroom. Two contiguous galleries, both painted black, approximate the size of the artists’ studios and distill the show’s thesis with luminous economy, leading viewers from the lyrical, early choreography of his pours, drips and stains to her smaller but exquisite Little Images—mosaic-like geometries painted with a palette knife.

From these sepulchral chambers the show opens to a large, high-ceilinged gallery flooded with daylight from newly revealed windows on Central Park. Here, Convergence hangs, backed with the Met’s prize Pollock, Autumn Rhythm: Number 30 (1950). The operatic shift in tone and scale drives home the outsize renown Pollock achieved after a 1949 feature in Life magazine posed the question, “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”

In the same gallery, tellingly, the eight collage paintings Krasner showed at Stable Gallery turn from the Pollocks to face each other like the stones of Stonehenge and look just as ritualistic, if more elated. After that, it’s back to black for a segment titled Re:Echo (after a Krasner), where Pollock’s arabesque, later works hang near her Robert Motherwell-like abstractions of the same period.

The rest of the show is all Krasner, but she outlived Pollock by 28 years. The swirling, abstracted floral landscapes became monumental, but appear in a few too many galleries, homogenizing their visual impact. The point—that no full understanding of one artist can come without the other—has already been made, capped by the one side-by-side juxtaposition: The Deep (1953), a chilling canvas where Pollock nearly obliterated a dark biomorph in clouds of white, and Birth (1956), an image of interlocking pink and black forms that Krasner painted the year he died. That pairing said it all.

Will this show correct a historic imbalance? Probably not market-wise, but a reputational correction seems both necessary and likely.

Installation view including Pollock's The Deep (1953)and Krasner's Birth (1956) in Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous

Photo by Anna-Marie Kellen; courtesy of The Met

The New York Times’s Holland Cotter describes the exhibition as an “exercise of art-historical reset”, and calls its installation of Pollocks “an entrancing sight”, while exulting in the “distinctive impression of personal joy” in Krasner’s post-Pollock work. In The Wall Street Journal, Karen Wilkin applauds the curators for encouraging “concentration on their work, rather than the mythology attached to both painters”, and on her Instagram, Jasper Johns’s biographer Deborah Solomon raves: “It’s like holding two opposed thoughts in your brain at the same time and wondering if your head will explode from the exhilaration of it all.”

#9072. SCAD alumni transform 18th-century staircase into colourful installation during Design Miami Paris

Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD) has revealed a colourful tufted flooring installation at this year’s Design Miami.Paris, as seen in this exclusive video produced by Dezeen.

Los Angeles-based designer and SCAD alumnus Abel Macias covered the staircase in fabric as part of a wider showcase of alumni works on display at the historic L’hôtel de Maisons in Paris.

Macias transformed the 18th-century staircase using bright colours and shapes informed by the landscape of the American Southwest.

At the top of the staircase, SCAD fibres graduate and Associate Chair of Fine Arts Gretchen Wagner presented a colourful suspended sculptural installation made from accordion-folded paper cylinders.

The paper cylinders were embellished with embroidered beading and hung from the ceiling like a chandelier.

SCAD furniture design graduate Evan Baker presented a wood-grain credenza, while SCAD furniture design graduate Anne Weber Callahan showed two ceramic stools meant to mimic clay.

Meanwhile, SCAD fibres graduate Katie Hagen designed a natural-dyed silk organza weaving, which was displayed alongside six sculptural lamps made by SCAD industrial design graduate Marcelo Suro.

The lamps merge hand-blown glass and volcanic stone and were created this past year by Suro during SCAD’s Alumni Atelier residency in Lacoste, France.

Macias completed a BFA illustration in 2002 and Wagner undertook an MFA in painting in 2023 and a BFA in fibres in 2011. Baker finished a BFA in furniture design in 2025, while Callahan graduated with a BFA in furniture design in 2019. Hagen obtained her MFA in fibres in 2023 and an MA in production design in 2023.

Last year, SCAD debuted an intricate plaster-cast installation at its booth during Design Miami in Florida.

SCAD is the official university partner of Design Miami and will next exhibit at the fair’s flagship event in Miami Beach this December.

To learn more about SCAD, visit its website.

Design Miami Paris took place from 20 to 25 October in Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

This video was produced by Dezeen as part of a partnership with SCAD. Find out more about Dezeen partnership content here.

Sony has revived a cult classic of 80s tech design, and retro fans are foaming at the mouth. And now they're back with a bang.

It shouldn't come as a surprise given the rising popularity of wired headphones. While it's only been a decade, we've come full circle, and now they're officially cool again. Sony's MDR-3R USB-C Wired Headphones are going for a tasty £49, but sadly they're currently sold out. But thankfully, if you're on the hunt for something similar, there are several popular dupes.

The new and improved MDR-3R's are all about preserving heritage. From the packaging to the design of the headphones themselves, there's a distinctly retro appeal to the design, but it's what's inside that counts. The open-air design creates a spacious, airy sound, offering natural, clear vocals and well-balanced sound with rich bass and extended highs.

Another retro competitor, the Koss Porta Pros offer elite sound with 60-ohm dynamic drivers, for sound clarity, rich bass, and an ultra-wide frequency response of 15–25,000 Hz. A premium, Koss-branded leatherette pouch offers easy portability thanks to the headphones' collapsible build. With a bolder design than the MDR-3Rs, these are wireless headphones built to stand out, perfect for retro lovers who want a unique, authentic look.

Wired EarPods have been having quite the style resurgence, spotted on celebrities like Bella Hadid, Harry Styles and Zendaya (check out @wireditgirls on Instagram for more). The effortless nonchalance of wired EarPods has made them the unshakable leader in the wired headphone game. Simple, clean and cool, they're a no-brainer if you want a more lowkey look.

Epic Games' Quixel Megascans has thousands of 3D models, decals and materials.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

No it's not a flashback to 2024, Epic Games has made its huge Quixel Megascans library free again, and this time it seems it's permanent. Access to the collection of photogrammetry-based 2D and 3D real-world assets was made free for a limited time two years ago to mark the launch of the Fab marketplace, but now it will be free indefinitely.

Quixel features thousands of production-ready items, including 3D models, tileable physically based rendering (PBR) surfaces, vegetation, decals, and custom materials, created by scanning real-world objects, environments. That makes it a massive resource for game developers, 3D artists, VFX artists and those working in architectural visualisation (also see our guides to the best laptops for CAD and the best laptops for 3D modelling).

The full Quixel Megascans library is going free. Fab listings will update between now & Nov 12, so check back if an asset you want isn’t free yet. We’ve updated terms for all Quixel assets so you can train AI models on Megascans & Megaplants. Learn more: https://t.co/jX1C4jRauw https://t.co/nuMDVwvJwcNovember 5, 2026

Megascans currently contains around 23,000 3D scanned assets. Quixel says listings on the Fab marketplace will be updated up until November 12 to make items free. It's also updated the terms for Quixel assets to allow Megascans and Megaplants assets to be used to train AI models.

"Your AI models can now learn from real-world scans to help you generate varied, photorealistic environments for your projects," it says.

Anyone who bought a Megascans or a Quixel Bundle on or after January 1, 2025 should receive a refund to their Epic Account Balance by the end of the year while keeping their licence and getting the new AI rights. The balance can be used across Epic's products, not just on Fab.

Epic has worked to make the new Fab marketplace as easy to use as possible; Channels can be used to discover compatible game engines while a mix of licences ensure you can find the right asset to meet your needs. Fab offers a Creative Commons licence and the Personal or Professional tier of a Standard License. Epic Games press release clarifies: "The Fab Standard License enables you to use the assets, including Megascans, in any game engine or tool you want."

Check out the Megascans library on Faby to see the variety of assets available, from furniture, and architecture to creature, vehicles and materials.

#9069. The World’s Best Biennial Is in St. Louis

A sign of the times: Shortly after St. Louis’s Counterpublic triennial chose sites for its third edition, climate disaster and civic disintegration plucked them off one by one. First was the International Institute, a nonprofit for immigrants and refugees selected after the last census showed that migrants made up the region’s only population growth. Originally, the team behind Counterpublic had hoped to highlight and celebrate the Institute’s vital work. But on Trump’s first day back in office, an executive order suspending refugee admissions decimated the organization’s budget, forcing it to furlough 60 percent of its staff. Related Articles Using the Graphics of GTA, Sara Sadik Explores the Challenges France's Muslim Youth Face Chicago Crowds Try and Fail to Move Anish Kapoor's Bean, Art Lawyer Michael Ward Stout Has Died, Louvre President Says Mona Lisa's Move Will Be Sad, and More

Then, a tornado ripped through The Ville, a redlined neighborhood, tearing the shingles off Sumner High School’s roof—which, despite being the first Black high school west of the Mississippi and boasting alumni such as Tina Turner, Dick Gregory, and Arthur Ashe,was already suffering from civic neglect. Next, a historic warehouse—one of the show’s main sites—caught fire: It smoldered all Black Friday weekend long, even through the snow, until its roof collapsed.

The question for the organizers of Counterpublic, a civically minded public art exhibition, became not only one of how to create site-specific, civically engaged artworks in the age of the poly-crisis, but why? Then, the existential threat wrought an existential reckoning that meaningfully reimagined what a recurring exhibition of the biennial/triennial variety might be.

The team titled the 2026 edition “Coyote Time,” after a video game that artist Alice Bucknell made for the show. The titular term refers to the grace-period moment after a character in a game runs off a cliff but before gravity catches up, when the player can still jump. It’s named for Wile E. Coyote, who hovers over the canyon until he looks down and clocks the height.

INFRASTRUCTURE HAS BECOME a central topic in art and politics of late, a theme of the most recent Whitney and Medina biennials and a focus of the Mamdani administration in New York. That’s largely because infrastructure becomes most visible when it isn’t working as it ought to—or when you’re not the person it’s designed to work for—as the curators of Counterpublic experienced vividly while selecting sites. For their exhibition, infrastructural critique became both subject and method.

At the International Institute, the curatorial cohort installed several new commissions thematically related to the Institute’s work. On the façade, Petrit Halilaj’s metallic monumentalization of children’s drawings from Kosovo harks back to his childhood as a refugee during the Yugoslav wars. Inside, Rachel Youn’s kinetic sculpture sees fake flowers move mechanically like the brushes of a car wash; theirs is an homage to immigrant labor (including their own family’s). To steward these artworks, Counterpublic also raised funds to hire back some furloughed staffand covered building upgrades, too: fresh paint, a new ceiling.

The artworks at the Institute are not simply a means to an end, nor a mere reversal of the art washing, tax evasion, and money laundering that have become part and parcel with art institutions. They also bring levity, dignity, and warmth to a space where migrants often spend hours waiting for legal counseling and paperwork help. The Institute is a life-giving center that nevertheless could have a perfunctory, bureaucratic feel. Counterpublic hoped to change that in a gesture that feels honest about the reality of what art can meaningfully bring forth, and also what it can’t. Material change and symbolic gestures are not the same, but they can work hand-in-hand.

One artwork, by Rirkrit Tiravanija, ties these threads together. It’s a continuation of his famous communal Thai food meals—quintessential biennial art—but the most delicious and most meaningful version I’ve encountered. The recipes were developed using native fruit, pawpaws, and with the help of the Institute’s clients, who in the process received training for potential careers in hospitality. Running through Counterpublic’s threemonths, the temporary restaurant offers free food and a space to gather. Counterpublic also helped support a new ventilation system and brought the Institute’s kitchen up to code, which set up Tiravanija’s project for success—and will also be useful for more cooking to come.

Tiravanija’s is a familiar project given new meaning by its context, much like the reimagined triennial format itself. While the artist’s original meal, first served in 1990, became a hallmark of relational aesthetics—a critique of the white cube’s reification of static objects through art that expanded to include social encounters—this version responded to a different kind of site and its needs. In so doing, it swapped institutional critique for infrastructural intervention. Here and throughout its three editions, Counterpublic has married art and action, always careful to parse activism from organizing.

AS IF DIRECTLY COUNTERING the criticism political art often (and rightly) gets for confusing virtue-signaling with substantive change, several artworks in Counterpublic aremore or less invisible: You could enjoy a free meal at the Institute without realizing you were consuming art at all. That is the trouble or the triumph—depending on who you ask—of systems artworks like these: The art part can be hard to see once the world around it gets blended in. In the exhibition’s catalog, artist Margaret Honda states outright that she wants her work to “be kind of invisible”: She installed two Noguchi-inspired benches and a brick path in The Ville alongside newly planted trees in response to the community’s request for parks.

Another inconspicuous artwork, Brianna Leatherbury’s Appreciation (2026), sees sculptures buried underground: Made of phosphate reclaimed by an agritech company from the city’s wastewaters, the works absorb lead and cleanse the soil. Without a Counterpublic sign, Leatherbury’s intervention would surely go unnoticed—and yet, it is among the projects that stayed with me most vividly. However invisible it may be, the work is also both a pollution solution and a symbol: Foursculptures are planted in The Ville, a Black neighborhood that bears traces of St. Louis’s disinvestment, and five morerun along the riverfront, home to a reserve of development ambitions. Both sites have been deemed “unoccupied” by the city, and Leatherbury’s project scrambles notions of waste and value: Fine art made from feces makes each lot less toxic and turns it into better real estate, but redlining and racism keep their market value uneven.

Two other works of latter-day Land art effect bioremediation, but blink and you’ll miss them: Chris Carlinstalled a garden of largely native plants and a subtle soundscape near Counterpublic’s main hub, and Lynne Smith rewilded a postindustrial pond at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC)—home to the nation’s largest collection of architectural artifacts, just across the Mississippi River in Illinois. NBAC inhabits a decommissioned steel foundry in what was once the company town of Monsanto—the chemical corporation we have to thank for DDT, Agent Orange, Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, and so much more. Foraging there for sumac berries one day, Smith came across a loading dock that had been converted into a retention pond for managing runoff, where frogs were laying eggs as young tadpoles slithered along. In an effort to make the site even more frog-friendly (and rehabilitate an arguably apocalyptic chemical crime scene), the artist installed a three-chamber structure—designed after the amphibian’s hearts—to filter rainwater and sediment, used to cultivate ancient native American lotus plants to mitigate both algae growth and the distinct chemical smells of the city.

Clearly, sustainability is a major theme of “Coyote Time,” but in more than just the ecological sense: The scale of the exhibition is considered and refreshingly humane for visitors, and every work by a living artist is a new commission. That means the organization does not take on more than it can meaningfully support, or give visitors more than they can meaningfully consume. Too often, biennial-goers leave beleaguered and artists end up in debt—suspended past the edge of the cliff in coyote time, wondering if it all will pay off.

Other memorable commissions include Li-Yi Fan’s absurdist video rating mirror renderings in various video games and Glenn Ligon’s riff on Thomas Jefferson’s famed feats of engineering—undulatingbrick walls that could stay sturdy with just one buttress-free layer—behind which he hid enslaved laborers. Titled Who Builds Anything In This Country (2026), Ligon’s work speaks to the enslaved labor that built St. Louis and its brick business, too;it is memorably installed just past St. Louis’s iconic Gateway Arch. Fan’s commission is sure to have afterlives in future exhibitions; Ligon’s is in St. Louis to stay.

Counterpublic’s models of redistribution, of art-as-infrastructure, and of sustainability find precedent, of course, in artists’ practices. Take duo Ryan Trecartin and Lizzie Fitch, who are part of the show: Whenthe sculptor and video artist received a major commission from Fondazione Prada for a 2019 exhibition, they used the funds to build a set—including a prefab barn with an amusement-park-like “lazy river”—where they now live and work. For “Coyote Time,” they created a similar structure blurring performance and life: A stage for the city that offers space for civic gathering, performing arts, and play. The duo’s signature frolicsome use of color and scale joins an equipment library with projectors, speakers, and microphones. The stage is one of 15 works—among them Honda’s, Ligon’s, Halilaj’s, Smith’s, and Carl’s—that is a permanent gift to the city.

ANYTHING THIS AMBITIOUS raises hard questions—in fact, that’s part of the point. One involves the slippery slope between well-meaning efforts to improve urban infrastructure and the gentrification that too often ensues. Where the displacement of poorer urban residents was once considered an unfortunate side effect of biennials and their ilk, we’ve now seen developers and municipalities enlist artists strategically for the purpose of increasing property value. Indeed, on opening night, I saw a lone protester with a sign that read our communites are not your brand.

But one could argue—indeed, Counterpublic seems to—that if we know art and real estate are now bedfellows, perhaps this can be wielded to a community’s advantage if organizers and not developers are at the helm. Certainly, this does seem worth a try. Notably, community partners—like The Ville’s 4theVille, on behalf of Sumner High School—reached out to Counterpublic to collaborate rather than the other way around. The school had nearly closed several times, but to remind the city of its cultural significance—which can seem at odds with its material neglect—Counterpublic commissioned Tony Cokes to craft a memorable homage to alumna Tina Turner, installed in a church nearby. And Timmy Simonds—whose ongoing project Miss Othmar School for Teachers imagines a school without students—made flags that pay homage to the first Black teachers college west of the Mississippi, once housed on the same site. A clever nod to how teachers—like the titular Miss Othmar, of Peanuts fame—are often only seen from the waist up, these pant-shaped former parachutes evoke their full personhood, while also dressing down the classroom’s hierarchy and the teacher’s authority. We’re all teachers and all students sometimes.

Where Counterpublic does make efforts to offer solutions to civic issues of varying scales, these gestures stand out for the way they never attempt to cover up the seams. Artworks lay issues bare as much as they attempt to ameliorate them, occupying an honest middle ground between critique and repair. Art, we all know, is hardly the ideal fix for civic issues, but still, solutions start somewhere. As Rebecca Solnit says, “revolution takes place first in the imagination,” or as (choose your fighter) Andrew Breitbart said, “politics is downstream from culture.” And yet, in “Coyote Time,” art is more than a start, because the exhibition is always thinking about what it leaves behind: a place to sit, a kitchen to cook in, a spot of shade, a stage to scream from, soil to grow in.
